docs.title: Ledoit & Wolf (2004) — Shrinkage Estimation
docs.text:
Ledoit, O., & Wolf, M. (2004). Honey, I Shrunk the Sample Covariance Matrix. The Journal of Portfolio Management, 30(4), 110–119. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2004.110

Contribution: Derived an analytically optimal shrinkage intensity for the sample covariance matrix, providing a closed-form, well-conditioned estimator that improves out-of-sample performance for Markowitz optimization.

Key formula: [ \hat{\Sigma}^{LW} = (1 - \alpha^) \hat{\Sigma} + \alpha^ \hat{\mu}_{cov} I ]

Implemented in: LedoitWolfEstimator

docs.title: Almgren & Chriss (2001) — Optimal Execution
docs.text:
Almgren, R., & Chriss, N. (2001). Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions. Journal of Risk, 3, 5–39. https://doi.org/10.21314/JOR.2001.041

Contribution: Derived an optimal trade execution strategy that minimizes total transaction costs (market impact + risk) for a given liquidation horizon. The market impact cost model is widely used in institutional portfolio management.

Market impact formula: [ \text{impact}_i = \gamma \sqrt{\frac{\text{trade_size}_i}{\text{daily_volume}_i}} ]

Implemented in: AlmgrenChrissCostModel

docs.title: Meucci (2008) — Fully Flexible Views: Theory and Practice
docs.text:
Meucci, A. (2008). Fully Flexible Views: Theory and Practice. Risk, 21(10), 97–102. https://ssrn.com/abstract=1213325

Contribution: Introduced Entropy Pooling to blend arbitrary non-Gaussian Monte Carlo distributions with linear equality and inequality views on returns, volatilities, and correlations via Relative Entropy (Kullback-Leibler) minimization solved in the low-dimensional Lagrange dual space.

Key formula: [ x^* = \arg\min_{x \in \Delta^M} \sum_{m=1}^M x_m \ln!\left(\frac{x_m}{p_m}\right) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad A x \le b, \; C x = d ]

Implemented in: EntropyPooler, ViewBuilder (AbsoluteView, RelativeView, VolatilityView, CovarianceView)

docs.title: Barone-Adesi, Giannopoulos & Vosper (1999) — Filtered Historical Simulation
docs.text:
Barone-Adesi, G., Giannopoulos, K., & Vosper, L. (1999). VaR Without Correlations for Portfolios of Derivative Securities. Journal of Futures Markets, 19(5), 583–602.

Contribution: Combined parametric GARCH volatility filtration with non-parametric historical residual bootstrapping, preserving empirical fat tails and cross-asset co-movement while adapting dynamically to current volatility regimes.

Implemented in: FHSGenerator

docs.title: McNeil & Frey (2000) & Demarta & McNeil (2005) — GARCH-EVT & Student-\(t\) Copula
docs.text:
McNeil, A. J., & Frey, R. (2000). Estimation of Tail-Related Risk Measures for Heteroscedastic Financial Time Series: An Extreme Value Approach. Journal of Empirical Finance, 7(3–4), 271–300.

Demarta, S., & McNeil, A. J. (2005). The \(t\) Copula and Related Copulas. International Statistical Review, 73(1), 111–129.

Contribution: Modeled conditional heteroscedasticity via AR-GARCH filtration, fitted Generalized Pareto Distributions (GPD) to extreme tail exceedances, and coupled marginals with a Student-\(t\) Copula to capture asymmetric tail risk and positive lower-tail crash dependence (\(\lambda_L > 0\)).

Implemented in: GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator

docs.title: Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2017) — Probability of Backtest Overfitting
docs.text:
Bailey, D. H., Borwein, J., López de Prado, M., & Zhu, Q. J. (2017). The Probability of Backtest Overfitting. Journal of Computational Finance, 20(4), 39–69. https://ssrn.com/abstract=2326253

Contribution: Introduced the non-parametric Combinatorial Symmetric Cross-Validation (CSCV) framework to estimate the probability that a strategy configuration selected for optimal In-Sample performance underperforms the median Out-of-Sample (\(\text{PBO} = \mathbb{P}[\lambda_c \le 0]\)).

Implemented in: PBOEvaluator, plot_pbo_distribution, RobustnessTearSheet

docs.title: López de Prado (2018) — Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation
docs.text:
López de Prado, M. (2018). Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley. (Chapter 12: Backtesting through Cross-Validation).

Contribution: Formulated Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV) to eliminate look-ahead leakage via purging and embargoing while generating \(\varphi(N, k) = \binom{N-1}{k-1}\) complete out-of-sample backtest paths across recombined market regimes.

Implemented in: CPCVSplitter, plot_cpcv_paths, RobustnessTearSheet

docs.title: Multi-Period Portfolio Optimization, Decision-Focused Learning & FinRL
Boyd, Busseti, Diamond, Kahn, Koh, Nystrup & Speth (2017) — Multi-Period Trading via Convex Optimization
docs.text:
Boyd, S., Busseti, E., Diamond, S., Kahn, R. N., Koh, K., Nystrup, P., & Speth, J. (2017). Multi-Period Trading via Convex Optimization. Foundations and Trends in Optimization, 3(1), 1–76. https://doi.org/10.1561/2400000023

Contribution: Unified multi-period portfolio optimization under a receding-horizon Model Predictive Control (MPC) convex program incorporating proportional bid-ask spread costs (\(\ell_1\)), square-root market impact (\(|z|^{3/2}\) power cones), holding costs, and terminal risk penalties.

Implemented in: MultiPeriodMPCAllocator, StochasticScenarioMPCAllocator

docs.title: Gârleanu & Pedersen (2013) — Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs
docs.text:
Gârleanu, N., & Pedersen, L. H. (2013). Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs. The Journal of Finance, 68(6), 2309–2340. https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12080

Contribution: Proved that under multi-horizon mean-reverting alpha signals and quadratic/permanent price impact, the optimal portfolio trades partially at a constant rate toward an intertemporal Aim Portfolio — a discounted weighted average of future Markowitz target portfolios.

Implemented in: AlphaDecayReturnEstimator, MultiPeriodMPCAllocator

docs.title: Elmachtoub & Grigas (2022) & Agrawal et al. (2019) — Decision-Focused Learning & Differentiable Convex Layers
docs.text:
Elmachtoub, A. N., & Grigas, P. (2022). Smart "Predict, then Optimize". Management Science, 68(1), 9–26.

Agrawal, A., Amos, B., Barratt, S., Boyd, S., Diamond, S., & Kolter, J. Z. (2019). Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 32.

Contribution: Formulated the convex SPO+ regret surrogate loss and implicit differentiation through fixed-point / KKT optimality conditions so neural predictors are trained directly on downstream multi-period decision utility.

Implemented in: MDFPOptimizationLayer, SPOPlusLoss, HybridDFLLoss, IPMOAllocator

docs.title: Buehler, Gonon, Teichmann & Wood (2019) & Liu et al. (2022) — Deep Hedging & FinRL
docs.text:
Buehler, H., Gonon, L., Teichmann, J., & Wood, B. (2019). Deep Hedging. Quantitative Finance, 19(8), 1271–1291.

Liu, X.-Y., Xia, Z., Rui, J., Gao, J., Yang, H., Zhu, M., Wang, C., Wang, Z., & Guo, J. (2022). FinRL-Meta: Market Environments and Benchmarks for Data-Driven Financial Reinforcement Learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 35.

Contribution: Formulated recurrent pathwise trajectory optimization under proportional/convex market frictions and standardized Gymnasium environments with Mahalanobis turbulence circuit-breakers for continuous portfolio control.

Implemented in: PortfolioGymEnv, ScenarioPortfolioEnv, TrajectoryPolicyNet, DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer, BayesianHRPAllocator, RLAllocator

docs.title: Moroke et al. (2026) — Thermodynamic & Bures-Wasserstein Regime Gating
docs.text:
Moroke, N., et al. (2026). Thermodynamic Efficiency Bounds and Wasserstein Optimal Transport in Non-Equilibrium Portfolio Rebalancing.

Contribution: Modeled portfolio rebalancing between fast and slow market covariance baths as a stochastic heat engine bounded by Carnot efficiency \(\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - T_{\min}/T_{\max}\), using the Bures-Wasserstein \(W_2\) distance to gate frictional turnover during structural regime ruptures.

Implemented in: WassersteinRegimeGate, ThermodynamicDiagnostics

docs.title: Generative Diffusion, Neural SDEs & Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization
Li (2023) — Wasserstein-Kelly Portfolios

Li, J. Y.-M. (2023). Wasserstein-Kelly Portfolios: A Robust Data-Driven Solution to Optimize Portfolio Growth. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.13979

Contribution: Formulated Distributionally Robust Kelly (log-optimal growth) portfolio optimization over a Wasserstein ball around the empirical distribution, proving tractable convex dual reformulations that prevent the extreme leverage and parameter sensitivity of classical Kelly portfolios.

Implemented in: WassersteinDROAllocator (ObjectiveFunction.WASSERSTEIN_KELLY)

docs.title: Fonseca & Junca (2021) & Esfahani & Kuhn (2018) — Wasserstein DRO with Expected Value Constraints

Fonseca, D., & Junca, M. (2021). Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization with Expected Value Constraints. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2111.04663

Mohajerin Esfahani, P., & Kuhn, D. (2018). Data-driven distributionally robust optimization using the Wasserstein metric: Performance guarantees and tractable reformulations. Mathematical Programming, 171(1–2), 115–166.

Contribution: Derived strong duality and finite convex program reformulations for worst-case expectation and CVaR minimization over Wasserstein balls intersected with linear expected-value constraints \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[G r] = q\), preserving all empirical data atoms while anchoring first-moment views.

docs.title: Cohen, Reisinger & Wang (2021) & Kidger et al. (2021) — Arbitrage-Free Neural SDE Market Models
docs.text:
Cohen, S. N., Reisinger, C., & Wang, S. (2021). Arbitrage-free neural-SDE market models. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2105.11053

Kidger, P., Foster, J., Li, X., & Lyons, T. J. (2021). Neural SDEs as Infinite-Dimensional GANs. International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML).

Contribution: Parameterized continuous-time asset price and implied-volatility factor SDEs with neural drift and diffusion coefficients subject to exact martingale / market-price-of-risk and calendar-spread no-arbitrage constraints, calibrated via pathwise rough-path signature discriminators.

Implemented in: NeuralSDEGenerator, NeuralSDEEstimator, ArbitrageFreeNeuralSDENet

Factor-Based Conditional Diffusion Model for Portfolio Optimization (2025). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2509.22088

Contribution: Formulated continuous-time entropy-regularized ("exploratory") reinforcement learning for mean-variance portfolio control under latent Markov regime switching, combining continuous-time Wonham regime belief filtering with analytical Gaussian exploration covariance \(\Sigma_{\pi, t}^* = (\lambda_{\text{ent}}/\gamma)(\bar{\Sigma}(p_t) + \kappa_{\text{turn}} I)^{-1}\).

Implemented in: ExploratoryRegimeMVAllocator, WonhamRegimeFilter

docs.title: Potapczynski et al. (2026) & Müller et al. (2022) — Time-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Networks (ApolloPFN) & Riemann Bar Posteriors
docs.text:
Potapczynski, A., Finzi, M., Goldblum, M., & Wilson, A. G. (2026). Time-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Time Series Forecasting (ApolloPFN). Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR). https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2603.15802

docs.text:
Blanchet, J., Kang, Y., & Murthy, K. (2019). Robust Wasserstein Profile Inference and Applications to Machine Learning. Journal of Applied Probability, 56(3), 830–857. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1610.05627

docs.title: Multi-Strategy Evaluation, Deflated Sharpe Ratio & Performance Attribution
Bailey & López de Prado (2014) — The Deflated Sharpe Ratio
docs.text:
Bailey, D. H., & López de Prado, M. (2014). The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality. The Journal of Portfolio Management, 40(5), 94–107. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2014.40.5.094

Contribution: Formulated the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) to correct for selection bias under multiple testing (\(N\) trials) and non-Normal return distributions (skewness \(\hat{\gamma}_3\) and kurtosis \(\hat{\gamma}_4\)), deriving the analytical expected maximum Sharpe hurdle \(\widehat{\text{SR}}_0\) via extreme value theory.

Key formula: [ \widehat{\text{SR}}_0 = \sqrt{\text{Var}[{\widehat{\text{SR}}_n}]} \left( (1 - \gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}!\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right) + \gamma\,\Phi^{-1}!\left(1 - \frac{1}{N e}\right) \right) ]

Implemented in: BacktestTracker, MultiStrategyComparator (BenchmarkSuite), MetricsTearSheet, compute_deflated_sharpe_ratio, ComparisonTearSheet

docs.title: Brinson & Fachler (1985) & Carino (1999) — Active Performance Attribution
docs.text:
Brinson, G. P., & Fachler, N. (1985). Measuring Non-U.S. Equity Portfolio Performance. The Journal of Portfolio Management, 11(3), 73–76. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.1985.409005

Carino, D. R. (1999). Combining Attribution Effects Over Time. The Journal of Performance Measurement, 3(4), 5–14.

Contribution: Decomposed active return \(R_p - R_b\) into Allocation, Selection, and Interaction effects across sectors or asset clusters, with logarithmic multi-period geometric linking so multi-period attribution sums exactly to total geometric active return.

Implemented in: PerformanceAttributor, BrinsonAttributionResult, plot_attribution_waterfall, ComparisonTearSheet

docs.title: Ma & Smith (2025) — Alpha Decay and Transaction Costs in Multi-Period Trading
docs.text:
Ma, C., & Smith, P. (2025). On the Effect of Alpha Decay and Transaction Costs on the Multi-period Optimal Trading Strategy. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2502.04284

Contribution: Analyzed the compounding interaction between multi-horizon alpha decay, intra-period weight drift, and linear/non-linear transaction costs when transitioning from theoretical paper signals to executed multi-period trajectories.

Implemented in: PerformanceAttributor.compute_frictional_drag, FrictionalDragResult, WalkForwardEngine, plot_attribution_waterfall

docs.title: Permutation-Invariant Set Transformers, Scalable-Softmax & Equivariant Portfolio Policies
Lee, Lee, Kim, Kosiorek, Choi & Teh (2019) — Set Transformer
docs.text:
Lee, J., Lee, Y., Kim, J., Kosiorek, A., Choi, S., & Teh, Y. W. (2019). Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks. Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 97, 3744–3753. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/lee19d/lee19d.pdf

Contribution: Formulated Multihead Attention Blocks (MAB), Set Attention Blocks (SAB), linear-time \(\mathcal{O}(Nm)\) Induced Set Attention Blocks (ISAB) via \(m\) trainable inducing points, and Pooling by Multihead Attention (PMA) as universal approximators of continuous permutation-equivariant and permutation-invariant functions on variable-cardinality sets.

Implemented in: MAB, SAB, ISAB, PMA, SetTransformerBackbone, SetTransformerCovarianceNet, SetTransformerPolicyNet

docs.title: Nakanishi (2025) & Martins & Astudillo (2016) — Scalable-Softmax (SSMax) & Sparsemax
docs.text:
Nakanishi, K. M. (2025). Scalable-Softmax Is Superior for Attention. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2501.19399

Martins, A. F. T., & Astudillo, R. F. (2016). From Softmax to Sparsemax: A Sparse Model of Attention and Multi-Label Classification. International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML).

Contribution: Proved that standard Softmax suffers from attention fading as set cardinality \(N\) scales, and introduced logarithmic logit scaling \(\operatorname{SSMax}(z_i; N, s) \propto \exp((s \ln N) z_i)\) alongside Euclidean simplex projections (Sparsemax / CappedSimplexProjection) to preserve concentration across 50-to-500 asset cardinality shifts.

Implemented in: ScalableMultiheadAttention, CappedSimplexProjection, UniverseSubsampler, plot_set_transformer_diagnostics

docs.title: Lin et al. (2021) & Bongiorno, Manolakis & Mantegna (2026) — Deep Risk Factor & RIE Spectral Covariance

Bongiorno, C., Manolakis, E., & Mantegna, R. N. (2026). End-to-End Large Portfolio Optimization for Variance Minimization. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2507.01918

Contribution: Formulated strictly congruence-equivariant low-rank factor-plus-diagonal PSD covariance heads (\(\hat{\Sigma}_t = B_t \Sigma_{F,t} B_t^\top + D_t\) with exact \(\mathcal{O}(Nm^2 + m^3)\) Woodbury inversion) and rotation-invariant eigenvalue spectral cleaning (RIESpectralHead) that generalize zero-shot across universe sizes.

Implemented in: ISABFactorDiagonalHead, EquivariantGramCorrHead, RIESpectralHead, SetTransformerCovarianceNet, WoodburyGaussianNLLLoss, WoodburySteinLoss

docs.title: Allocators
docs.text: Allocators solve for optimal portfolio weights given market data, a covariance matrix, and optionally expected returns. All allocators implement BaseAllocator and can be dropped into any StrategyPipeline.

docs.title: Equal Weight, Inverse Volatility & Market Cap Baselines
docs.text:
PyAlloq provides four fast analytical baselines in pyalloq.classical.optimizers.naive:

  • EqualWeightAllocator: Assigns identical weight \(1/N\) to every asset.
  • InverseVolatilityAllocator: Assigns weights inversely proportional to standalone asset volatility \(w_i \propto 1/\sigma_i\) (ignoring cross-correlations).
  • MarketCapWeightAllocator: Assigns weights proportional to data.cross_sectional["market_cap"] (or falls back to \(1/N\)).
  • RandomAllocator: Samples simplex weights from a symmetric Dirichlet distribution.
\[ w_i^{\text{EW}} = \frac{1}{N}, \qquad w_i^{\text{IV}} = \frac{1/\sigma_i}{\sum_{j=1}^N 1/\sigma_j}, \qquad w_i^{\text{MCap}} = \frac{\text{MCap}_i}{\sum_{j=1}^N \text{MCap}_j} \] 
from pyalloq import (
    EqualWeightAllocator,
    InverseVolatilityAllocator,
    MarketCapWeightAllocator,
    StrategyPipeline,
)

pipeline_ew = StrategyPipeline(allocator=EqualWeightAllocator(tickers=data.assets))
pipeline_iv = StrategyPipeline(allocator=InverseVolatilityAllocator(tickers=data.assets))
pipeline_mc = StrategyPipeline(allocator=MarketCapWeightAllocator(tickers=data.assets))

Use as baselines

Always include EqualWeightAllocator and InverseVolatilityAllocator as benchmarks in your backtest comparisons.

docs.title: Markowitz (MarkowitzAllocator)
docs.text:
Classical mean-variance optimizer supporting five objectives (MIN_VOLATILITY, MAX_SHARPE, MAX_RETURN, EFFICIENT_RETURN, EFFICIENT_RISK), institutional constraints, and efficient frontier tracing.

from pyalloq import MarkowitzAllocator, ObjectiveFunction
Min VolatilityMax SharpeMax Return (Utility)Efficient Return & Efficient RiskConstraints (Bounds, Market-Neutral, Sectors, Turnover)

Minimizes total portfolio variance with no expected return input needed.

\[ \min_w \; w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1,\; w \geq 0 \] 
allocator = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY
)

Maximizes the Sharpe ratio using the homogenized Cornuéjols-Tütüncü / Tobin transformation. Requires expected returns.

\[ \max_w \frac{w^\top \mu - r_f}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} \;\equiv\; \min_{y, \kappa \ge 0} \; y^\top \Sigma y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad (\mu - r_f)^\top y = 1,\; \mathbf{1}^\top y = \kappa \] 
allocator = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE
)
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
)

Maximizes mean-variance utility, controlled by risk_aversion in MarketData.

\[ \max_w \; \mu^\top w - \lambda \cdot w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1,\; w \geq 0 \] 
allocator = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_RETURN
)

Target a specific expected return (EFFICIENT_RETURN) or volatility ceiling (EFFICIENT_RISK), or trace the entire Efficient Frontier:

# Minimize volatility subject to portfolio return >= 12%
alloc_ret = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.EFFICIENT_RETURN,
    target_return=0.12,
)

# Maximize expected return subject to portfolio volatility <= 15%
alloc_risk = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.EFFICIENT_RISK,
    target_volatility=0.15,
)

# Trace 20 portfolios along the Efficient Frontier
frontier_results = alloc_ret.efficient_frontier(
    data, cov_matrix=cov, expected_returns=mu, n_points=20
)

MarkowitzAllocator natively supports box bounds, dollar-neutrality, gross leverage limits, single-period turnover limits, L2 diversification regularization, and sector caps/floors:

constrained_allocator = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE,
    weight_bounds=(0.02, 0.35),                     # Per-asset min/max bounds
    market_neutral=False,                           # Set True for sum(w) == 0
    max_leverage=1.0,                               # L1 gross leverage ||w||_1 <= L
    max_turnover=0.40,                              # ||w - w_prev||_1 <= 0.40
    l2_gamma=0.01,                                  # L2 weight regularization
    sector_mapper={"AAPL": "Tech", "MSFT": "Tech", "JPM": "Finance"},
    sector_upper={"Tech": 0.50},
    sector_lower={"Finance": 0.15},
)

docs.title: Conditional Value-at-Risk & Drawdown (MeanCVaRAllocator & CDaRAllocator)
docs.text:
When asset returns exhibit fat tails or negative skewness, variance-based optimization underestimates tail risk. PyAlloq provides two single-period linear/conic downside risk allocators in pyalloq.classical.optimizers.cvar:

  • MeanCVaRAllocator: Minimizes portfolio Expected Shortfall (\(\text{CVaR}_\beta\)) via the Rockafellar & Uryasev (2000) linear program (supports MIN_CVAR, EFFICIENT_RETURN, and MAX_RETURN objectives plus box bounds, market neutrality, turnover, and L2 regularization).
  • CDaRAllocator: Minimizes Conditional Drawdown-at-Risk (\(\text{CDaR}_\beta\)) over the historical cumulative return path (Chekhlov, Uryasev & Zabarankin, 2005).
from pyalloq import CDaRAllocator, MeanCVaRAllocator, ObjectiveFunction

# 95% CVaR minimization with 40% per-asset cap
cvar_allocator = MeanCVaRAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    beta=0.95,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_CVAR,
    weight_bounds=(0.0, 0.40),
)

# 90% Conditional Drawdown-at-Risk minimization
cdar_allocator = CDaRAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    beta=0.90,
    weight_bounds=(0.0, 0.50),
)

docs.title: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization (WassersteinDROAllocator)
docs.text:
Optimizes portfolio weights against the worst-case return distribution \(\mathbb{Q}\) inside a Wasserstein ambiguity ball \(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon_t}(\hat{\mathbb{P}})\) centered at either historical returns (MarketData) or synthetic 3D trajectory tensors (ScenarioMarketData), optionally intersected with Fonseca & Junca (2021) linear expected-value constraints \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[G r] = q\):

  • ObjectiveFunction.WASSERSTEIN_KELLY (Li, 2023): Maximizes worst-case expected geometric log-growth \(\inf_{\mathbb{Q}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[\ln(1 + \eta r^\top w)]\) with optional fractional Kelly scaling kelly_fraction.
  • ObjectiveFunction.WASSERSTEIN_CVAR (Esfahani & Kuhn, 2018): Minimizes worst-case Conditional Value-at-Risk (\(\text{CVaR}_\beta\)) over the Wasserstein ball.
  • ObjectiveFunction.WASSERSTEIN_MEAN_RISK: Maximizes worst-case expected return minus worst-case CVaR.
  • Geometry-Aware Ground Metrics (ground_metric): Supports "mahalanobis" (dual norm \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}(w - G^\top \lambda)\|_2\)), "quantile_mahalanobis" (Blanchet, Kang & Murthy 2019 anisotropic transport geometry calibrated to the Riemann Bar inter-decile spread \(q_{0.90} - q_{0.10}\) and negative Bowley skewness), "l2", and "l1".
  • Dynamic Optimal-Transport Radius (radius_mode="regime_adaptive"): Automatically scales \(\varepsilon_t = \varepsilon + \kappa \cdot W_2(\mathcal{N}_{\text{fast}}, \mathcal{N}_{\text{slow}})\) using WassersteinRegimeGate.
import numpy as np
from pyalloq import ObjectiveFunction, WassersteinDROAllocator

# 1. Wasserstein-Kelly Portfolio with adaptive regime-shift radius
kelly_dro = WassersteinDROAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.WASSERSTEIN_KELLY,
    epsilon=0.005,
    ground_metric="mahalanobis",
    radius_mode="regime_adaptive",
    kelly_fraction=0.5,
)
res_kelly = kelly_dro.allocate(data)

# 2. Worst-Case Mean-CVaR with Fonseca & Junca (2021) expected-value view constraints
view_G = np.array([[1.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.0]])  # Asset 0 outperforms Asset 1
view_q = np.array([0.0008])                 # by +8 bps/day in expectation
view_dro = WassersteinDROAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.WASSERSTEIN_MEAN_RISK,
    epsilon=0.005,
    view_matrix=view_G,
    view_targets=view_q,
)
res_view = view_dro.allocate(data)

docs.title: Risk Parity (RiskParityAllocator)
docs.text:
Equal Risk Contribution (ERC). Every asset contributes the same amount of marginal risk to the portfolio. No expected return input needed — purely covariance-driven.

\[ \min_y \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \ln y_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y \geq 0 \]

Then normalize: \(w = y / \mathbf{1}^\top y\)

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Risk Budgeting (RiskBudgetingAllocator)
docs.text:
Generalization of Risk Parity where each asset is assigned a target risk budget \(b_i\). If no budgets are provided, defaults to equal budgeting (identical to Risk Parity).

\[ \min_y \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} b_i \ln y_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y \geq 0 \] 
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_budgeting import RiskBudgetingAllocator
import pandas as pd

# Provide risk budgets through MarketData.features
risk_budgets = pd.DataFrame(
    {"AAPL": [0.4], "MSFT": [0.3], "GOOGL": [0.3]},
    index=data.prices.index[:1]
).reindex(data.prices.index).ffill()

data_with_budgets = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices,
    features={"risk_budgets": risk_budgets},
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskBudgetingAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Max Diversification (MaxDiversificationAllocator)
docs.text:
Maximizes the Diversification Ratio — the weighted sum of individual asset volatilities divided by portfolio volatility.

\[ \max_w \; D(w) = \frac{w^\top \sigma}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} \]

Implemented via the equivalent dual: minimize portfolio variance subject to weighted volatilities summing to 1.

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.max_diversification import MaxDiversificationAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MaxDiversificationAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Graph-Based ML Allocators
docs.text: These allocators use hierarchical clustering on the correlation matrix to build a dendrogram-based weight allocation. They do not invert the covariance matrix, making them more numerically stable for large universes.

docs.title: HRP (HRPAllocator)
docs.text:
Hierarchical Risk Parity (López de Prado, 2016). Uses single-linkage clustering on correlation distance, quasi-diagonalization of the covariance matrix, and recursive bisection to assign inverse-variance weights.

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.hrp import HRPAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=HRPAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

Steps: 1. Compute correlation distance matrix: \(d_{ij} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \rho_{ij}}{2}}\) 2. Build hierarchical cluster tree (dendrogram) 3. Sort assets by quasi-diagonalization 4. Assign weights via recursive bisection using cluster inverse-variance portfolios

docs.title: Spectral Graph Laplacian HRP (SpectralLaplacianHRPAllocator)
docs.text:
Instead of single-linkage agglomerative clustering (which can suffer from "chaining" artifacts), SpectralLaplacianHRPAllocator (or HRPAllocator(clustering_mode="spectral_laplacian")) performs recursive Fiedler vector (\(v_2\)) spectral sweep cuts on the normalized Graph Laplacian \(\mathcal{L}_S = I - D_S^{-1/2} W_S D_S^{-1/2}\) of each induced subgraph, with an optional fragility penalty tilting capital away from sub-graphs with high internal algebraic connectivity \(\lambda_2(\mathcal{L}_S)\):

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers import SpectralLaplacianHRPAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=SpectralLaplacianHRPAllocator(
        tickers=data.assets,
        fragility_penalty=0.25,
    )
)

docs.title: HERC (HERCAllocator)
docs.text:
Hierarchical Equal Risk Contribution. Similar to HRP but allocates risk budget equally across the hierarchical clusters at each level, then inverse-variance within each cluster.

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.herc import HERCAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=HERCAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: NCO (NCOAllocator)
docs.text:
Nested Cluster Optimization. Divides the universe into clusters via k-means on the correlation matrix, runs a Markowitz optimization within each cluster (intra-cluster), and then a second Markowitz optimization across cluster representatives (inter-cluster).

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.nco import NCOAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=NCOAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Size-Invariant Set Transformer End-to-End Policies (SetTransformerPolicyNet & DeepAllocator)
docs.text:
SetTransformerPolicyNet implements PyAlloq's BasePolicyNetwork (forward(x, w_current=None, mask=None, attn_bias=None) -> w_target) using Induced Set Attention Blocks (ISAB), Pooling by Multihead Attention (PMA_1), and Scalable-Softmax (SSMax). A policy trained on a 500-stock universe with UniverseSubsampler transfers zero-shot to a 50-stock inference subset without tensor shape errors or Softmax concentration collapse.

It supports five strictly equivariant, mask-aware mandate output heads:

  • mandate="capped_simplex" (CappedSimplexProjection): Exact vectorized bisection projection onto \(\{w : \sum_i w_i = 1, 0 \le w_i \le w_{\max}\}\) with zero weight on padded/untradable slots.
  • mandate="sparsemax": Exact Euclidean simplex projection (\(w_{\max} = 1\)) inducing sparse active holdings.
  • mandate="masked_dirichlet" (MaskedDirichletCashHead): Simplex concentration parameters over active assets plus an invariant cash logit derived from the PMA_1 [REGIME] token (for POMDPPortfolioEnv and SB3PortfolioAgent(policy_backbone="set_transformer")).
  • mandate="dollar_neutral" (DollarNeutralStatArbHead): Strictly zero net exposure (\(\sum_i w_i = 0\)) and exact target gross leverage (\(\sum_i |w_i| = G_{\text{gross}}\)) across any active asset count.
  • mandate="vol_targeted" (VolTargetedContinuousRiskHead): Directional risk weights scaled by inverse asset volatility \(1 / \hat{\sigma}_{i,t}\).
from pyalloq import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.dl import DeepAllocator, SetTransformerPolicyNet

policy_net = SetTransformerPolicyNet(
    n_features=1,
    hidden_dim=64,
    num_heads=4,
    num_inds=16,
    mandate="capped_simplex",
    max_weight=0.20,
    temporal_type="vsn_conv",
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=DeepAllocator(
        model=policy_net,
        lookback_window=30,
        tickers=data.assets,
    )
)

docs.title: Choosing an Allocator
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Allocator Quick analytical baselines EqualWeightAllocator, InverseVolatilityAllocator, MarketCapWeightAllocator Minimize portfolio risk, no return forecast needed RiskParityAllocator Minimize portfolio risk, trust your return forecast MarkowitzAllocator(MIN_VOLATILITY) Maximize Sharpe with box/sector/turnover constraints MarkowitzAllocator(MAX_SHARPE, weight_bounds=..., sector_upper=...) Target return or target volatility / Efficient Frontier MarkowitzAllocator(EFFICIENT_RETURN) / MarkowitzAllocator(EFFICIENT_RISK) Heavy-tailed downside or drawdown control MeanCVaRAllocator or CDaRAllocator Structural breaks, regime shifts, or worst-case log-growth (Kelly) WassersteinDROAllocator (WASSERSTEIN_KELLY / WASSERSTEIN_CVAR) Large universe (50+ assets), covariance unstable HRPAllocator, NCOAllocator, or BayesianHRPAllocator Maximize portfolio diversification MaxDiversificationAllocator Assign specific risk budgets per asset RiskBudgetingAllocator

docs.title: Converting Continuous Weights to Integer Shares (DiscreteShareAllocator)
docs.text:
In live trading, continuous portfolio weights \(w \in \mathbb{R}^N\) must be converted into whole share or lot orders given current asset prices and total account cash. DiscreteShareAllocator supports both method="greedy" and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (method="lp"), handling both long-only and long-short portfolios:

from pyalloq import DiscreteShareAllocator

weights = pipeline.generate_weights(data)

disc = DiscreteShareAllocator(total_portfolio_value=100_000.0, lot_size=1)
order_plan = disc.allocate(weights, latest_prices=data, method="greedy")

print(order_plan.shares)          # {'AAPL': 142, 'MSFT': 88, 'GOOGL': 115, ...}
print(order_plan.leftover_cash)   # 43.18
print(order_plan.rmse_error)      # 0.0004

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Allocator
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.interfaces import BaseAllocator
from pyalloq_core.results import OptimizationResult
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyCustomAllocator(BaseAllocator):
    def allocate(
        self,
        data: MarketData,
        cov_matrix: pd.DataFrame,
        expected_returns: pd.Series | None = None,
        **kwargs,
    ) -> OptimizationResult:
        # Your optimization logic here
        weights = pd.Series(1.0 / len(data.assets), index=data.assets)
        return OptimizationResult(weights=weights, status="OPTIMAL")

# Drop it into any pipeline — no other changes needed
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=MyCustomAllocator(tickers=data.assets))

docs.title: Backtesting
docs.text: WalkForwardEngine runs your StrategyPipeline across historical data, rebalancing at regular intervals, and accounts for transaction costs — with a zero-lookahead guarantee at every step.

docs.title: WalkForwardEngine
docs.text:
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",                        # monthly rebalancing
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(252),         # 1-year rolling lookback
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(bps=10.0),       # 10 bps per trade
)

results = engine.run(data)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description pipeline StrategyPipeline required The strategy to backtest rebalance_freq str "ME" Pandas offset alias: "ME" (monthly), "W" (weekly), "QE" (quarterly) splitter BaseWindowSplitter RollingWindowSplitter(252) Controls how historical windows are sliced cost_model BaseCostModel FlatBpsCostModel(10.0) Transaction cost model applied at each rebalance

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
results = engine.run(data)

results["returns"]     # pd.Series — daily portfolio returns (net of costs)
results["weights"]     # pd.DataFrame — daily forward-filled weights
results["tear_sheet"]  # pd.DataFrame — performance summary

docs.title: Window Splitters
docs.text: The splitter controls how much historical data is visible to the pipeline at each rebalance date.

docs.title: Rolling Window (RollingWindowSplitter)
docs.text:
Uses a fixed-length lookback window. The window slides forward with each rebalance. Only rebalance dates with enough history (≥ lookback_window observations) are included.

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import RollingWindowSplitter

# Use exactly 1 year (252 trading days) of history at each rebalance
splitter = RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=252)

When to use: You want a consistent amount of data at each period, ignoring older observations. Appropriate for estimators sensitive to regime change.

docs.title: Expanding Window (ExpandingWindowSplitter)
docs.text:
Uses all available history up to each rebalance date, with a minimum threshold to start.

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import ExpandingWindowSplitter

# Start backtesting once 252 days of data are available; use all history thereafter
splitter = ExpandingWindowSplitter(min_periods=252)

When to use: When longer history improves estimator stability (e.g., Ledoit-Wolf, sample covariance), and you don't expect structural breaks.

docs.title: Purged K-Fold (PurgedKFoldSplitter)
docs.text:
Used for ML model training and cross-validation, not for backtesting. Splits data into K folds and applies an embargo (gap between train and test sets) to prevent information leakage from overlapping return windows.

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import PurgedKFoldSplitter

splitter = PurgedKFoldSplitter(n_splits=5, embargo_pct=0.01)

for train_data, test_data in splitter.split(data):
    model.fit(train_data)
    predictions = model.predict(test_data)

Not for standard backtesting

PurgedKFoldSplitter is designed for ML training loops, not for WalkForwardEngine. Use RollingWindowSplitter or ExpandingWindowSplitter for standard portfolio backtests.

docs.title: Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation & Scrambling (CPCVSplitter & PBOEvaluator)
docs.text:
To guard against backtest overfitting and chronological regime luck, pyalloq-backtest includes Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCVSplitter) and Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBOEvaluator):

  1. Regime Scrambling (CPCVSplitter.scramble_timelines): Partitions historical strategy returns into \(N\) chronological regime blocks and recombines them into scrambled timelines to test whether a strategy's Sharpe ratio and drawdowns survive when the sequence of market regimes is reordered.
  2. Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBOEvaluator):
  3. evaluate_cscv(strategy_returns_matrix): Runs Bailey & López de Prado's Combinatorial Symmetric Cross-Validation (CSCV) across a \((T \times M)\) matrix of \(M\) strategy trials to compute the exact probability that the In-Sample optimal strategy underperforms the median Out-of-Sample (\(\mathbb{P}[\lambda_c \le 0]\)).
  4. evaluate_benchmark(historical_result, cpcv_or_mc_result): Evaluates a single strategy's historical Sharpe against a distribution of CPCV or Monte Carlo paths.
from pyalloq_backtest import CPCVSplitter, PBOEvaluator

# 1. Scramble historical backtest across 6 regime blocks
cpcv = CPCVSplitter(n_groups=6, k_test_groups=2, max_paths=100)
cpcv_result = cpcv.scramble_timelines(results)

# 2. Evaluate single-strategy survival vs. scrambled timelines
pbo_eval = PBOEvaluator(n_partitions=8)
pbo_bench = pbo_eval.evaluate_benchmark(results, cpcv_result)
print(f"Prob(OOS Sharpe < 0): {pbo_bench.prob_oos_loss:.1%}")

Interactive Robustness Visualizations

Pass results, cpcv_result, or pbo_result directly to RobustnessTearSheet in pyalloq-viz to plot Rank Logit distributions, IS-vs-OOS Sharpe degradation, and scrambled equity cones.

docs.title: Flat Bps (FlatBpsCostModel)
docs.text:
A flat percentage fee applied to the absolute change in weights at each rebalance. Suitable for retail or small-AUM use cases.

\[ \text{cost}_i = |\Delta w_i| \times \frac{\text{bps}}{10000} \] 
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import FlatBpsCostModel

cost_model = FlatBpsCostModel(bps=10.0)  # 10 basis points per unit of turnover

docs.title: Almgren-Chriss (AlmgrenChrissCostModel)
docs.text:
Non-linear market impact cost model. Models both fixed bid-ask spread and non-linear price impact proportional to trade size relative to daily volume.

\[ \text{cost}_i = \left(\text{spread} + \gamma \sqrt{\frac{\text{trade\_size}_i}{\text{volume}_i}}\right) \times |\Delta w_i| \] 
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import AlmgrenChrissCostModel

cost_model = AlmgrenChrissCostModel(
    portfolio_aum=1_000_000,  # portfolio size in USD
    spread_bps=2.0,            # bid-ask spread
    gamma=0.1,                 # market impact coefficient
)

Requires volume data

AlmgrenChrissCostModel requires data.features["volume"] to be set on your MarketData. Volume is used to compute trade size as a fraction of daily market volume.

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,
    features={"volume": volume_df},
)

docs.title: Performance Metrics (TearSheet)
docs.text:
MetricsTearSheet.generate(portfolio_returns) produces a summary table of key performance metrics.

Metric Formula Description total_return \((1+r)^{T} - 1\) Cumulative return over full period annualized_return \((1 + \text{total\_return})^{1/Y} - 1\) Geometric annualized return annualized_volatility \(\sigma_r \times \sqrt{252}\) Annualized standard deviation sharpe_ratio \(\frac{r_a - r_f}{\sigma_a}\) Risk-adjusted return probabilistic_sharpe_ratio \(\Phi\!\left(\frac{(\widehat{SR} - SR^*)\sqrt{T-1}}{\sqrt{1 - \hat{\gamma}_3 \widehat{SR} + \frac{\hat{\gamma}_4 - 1}{4}\widehat{SR}^2}}\right)\) Probability that Sharpe exceeds target \(SR^*\) deflated_sharpe_ratio \(\text{PSR}(\widehat{SR}_0)\) Probability that Sharpe is statistically significant after penalizing for \(N\) trials, skewness, and kurtosis expected_max_sharpe_ratio \(\widehat{SR}_0(N, \text{Var}[\{\widehat{SR}_n\}])\) Expected maximum Sharpe hurdle under the False Strategy Theorem maximum_drawdown \(\min_t \frac{V_t - \max_{\tau \leq t} V_\tau}{\max_{\tau \leq t} V_\tau}\) Largest peak-to-trough decline calmar_ratio (\frac{r_a}{ \text{MDD} 
from pyalloq_backtest.metrics import MetricsTearSheet

tear_sheet = MetricsTearSheet.generate(
    portfolio_returns=results["returns"],
    risk_free_rate=0.04,
)
print(tear_sheet)

docs.title: Multi-Strategy Comparison & Deflated Sharpe Ratio (BenchmarkSuite)
docs.text:
Evaluating multiple allocators simultaneously on the same historical trajectory introduces Selection Bias (the Multiple Testing Problem). pyalloq-backtest solves this via two integrated components:

  1. BacktestTracker (Singleton Ledger): Thread-safe singleton inside WalkForwardEngine that automatically increments the trial counter \(N\) and records each executed pipeline's Sharpe ratio, skewness, and kurtosis so cross-trial variance \(\text{Var}[\{\widehat{\text{SR}}_n\}]\) and the False Strategy hurdle \(\widehat{\text{SR}}_0\) are tracked automatically.
  2. MultiStrategyComparator (BenchmarkSuite): Runs a dictionary of StrategyPipeline (or WalkForwardEngine) instances concurrently over identical MarketData (and optional ScenarioMarketData), outputting a ComparisonResult with .summary_table, .results, .scenario_results, and .attributions.
from pyalloq_backtest import BacktestTracker, BenchmarkSuite, RollingWindowSplitter, AlmgrenChrissCostModel
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.classical import EqualWeightAllocator, RiskParityAllocator, MarkowitzAllocator, MultiPeriodMPCAllocator, LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq.ml import HRPAllocator

pipelines = {
    "EqualWeight": StrategyPipeline(allocator=EqualWeightAllocator(tickers=data.assets)),
    "RiskParity": StrategyPipeline(allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets), cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage()),
    "HRP": StrategyPipeline(allocator=HRPAllocator(tickers=data.assets), cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage()),
    "Markowitz": StrategyPipeline(allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets), cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage()),
    "MultiPeriodMPC": StrategyPipeline(allocator=MultiPeriodMPCAllocator(tickers=data.assets), cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage()),
}

with BacktestTracker.session(reset=True) as tracker:
    suite = BenchmarkSuite(
        pipelines=pipelines,
        splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=252),
        cost_model=AlmgrenChrissCostModel(portfolio_aum=10_000_000, spread_bps=4.0, gamma=0.1),
        rebalance_freq="ME",
        benchmark="EqualWeight",
    )
    comp_result = suite.run(data)
    print(f"Total Trials Accounted (N): {tracker.n_trials}")
    print(comp_result.summary_table[["annualized_return", "sharpe_ratio", "deflated_sharpe_ratio", "maximum_drawdown"]])

docs.title: Brinson-Fachler, Factor & Frictional Drag Attribution (PerformanceAttributor)
docs.text:
To prove whether an allocator's outperformance stems from genuine skill, passive factor beta, or is eroded by execution mechanics, PerformanceAttributor decomposes active return \(R_p - R_b\) across three pillars:

  1. Classical Brinson-Fachler Decomposition (compute_brinson_fachler):
  2. Decomposes active return into Allocation Effect, Selection Effect, and Interaction Effect across sectors or hierarchical asset clusters.
  3. Supports Carino (1999) geometric multi-period linking (default) and arithmetic linking, with a 3-tier cluster resolution hierarchy (explicit sector_map \(\rightarrow\) MarketData.cross_sectional["sector"] \(\rightarrow\) automatic Ward/HRP correlation clustering).
  4. Factor-Implied Attribution (compute_factor_attribution):
  5. Regresses active returns against systematic risk premia (Market, Momentum, LowVolatility, plus Size and Value when available, or custom factor_returns) using OLS with Newey-West HAC \(t\)-statistics.
  6. Frictional Drag Accounting (compute_frictional_drag, Ma & Smith, 2025):
  7. Bridges Theoretical Paper Return (un-drifted target weights) \(\rightarrow\) Alpha Decay & Drift Drag \(\rightarrow\) Gross Executed Return \(\rightarrow\) Proportional Spread/Commission Drag \(\rightarrow\) Almgren-Chriss Square-Root Market Impact Drag \(\rightarrow\) Short Borrow Drag \(\rightarrow\) Net Realized Return.
from pyalloq_backtest import PerformanceAttributor

attributor = PerformanceAttributor(linking_method="carino", hac_lags=5)
attr_res = attributor.attribute(
    backtest_result=comp_result.results["MultiPeriodMPC"],
    market_data=data,
    benchmark_weights=comp_result.results["EqualWeight"],
)

print(attr_res.brinson.sector_summary)        # Allocation, Selection, Interaction by sector/cluster
print(attr_res.factor.factor_summary)         # Factor exposures, Newey-West t-stats, annualized alpha
print(attr_res.frictional.waterfall_summary)  # Paper -> Drift/Decay -> Spread -> Market Impact -> Net

docs.title: Full Backtest Example
docs.text:
from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine
from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import ExpandingWindowSplitter
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import AlmgrenChrissCostModel

data = YahooFinanceClient().get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN"],
    start="2018-01-01", end="2024-01-01",
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
)

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",
    splitter=ExpandingWindowSplitter(min_periods=252),
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(bps=5.0),
)

results = engine.run(data)
print(results["tear_sheet"])

docs.title: Covariance Estimators
docs.text:
Covariance estimators produce an NxN annualized covariance matrix from a MarketData object. The choice of estimator has a major impact on optimizer stability, especially for Markowitz-family allocators.

All estimators implement BaseCovarianceEstimator:

class BaseCovarianceEstimator(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.DataFrame:
        ...

docs.title: Empirical (EmpiricalCovariance)
docs.text:
The classical sample covariance matrix. Simple and unbiased, but sensitive to outliers and unreliable when the number of observations \(T\) is close to the number of assets \(N\).

\[ \hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{T-1} \sum_{t=1}^{T} (r_t - \bar{r})(r_t - \bar{r})^\top \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.empirical import EmpiricalCovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=EmpiricalCovariance(),
)

When to use: Large \(T/N\) ratio (e.g., 10+ years of daily data for 20 stocks). Stable, liquid markets.

docs.title: EWMA (EWMACovariance)
docs.text:
Exponentially Weighted Moving Average covariance. More recent observations receive exponentially higher weight, capturing volatility clustering (GARCH-like behaviour).

\[ \hat{\Sigma}_t = (1-\lambda) r_{t} r_{t}^\top + \lambda \hat{\Sigma}_{t-1} \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ewma import EWMACovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=EWMACovariance(span=120),  # 120-day span
)

When to use: Volatile or crisis periods where recent correlations matter more. Time-varying risk models.

docs.title: Ledoit-Wolf (LedoitWolfShrinkage)
docs.text:
Analytically optimal shrinkage of the sample covariance towards a structured target (e.g., identity or scaled identity). Minimizes mean squared error of the estimator.

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{LW} = (1 - \alpha^*) \hat{\Sigma} + \alpha^* \mu \mathbf{I} \]

where \(\alpha^*\) is the analytically derived optimal shrinkage intensity.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
)

When to use: High-dimensional portfolios (\(N > 50\)), short histories. The go-to robust estimator for Markowitz optimization.

See: Ledoit & Wolf (2004)

docs.title: Random Matrix Theory (RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator)
docs.text:
Filters the empirical covariance matrix by removing noise eigenvalues that fall below the Marchenko-Pastur upper bound. These eigenvalues are statistical artifacts of finite sample size, not true economic factors.

Denoising step: Any eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) below the Marchenko-Pastur bound \(\lambda_+\) is replaced by the average noise eigenvalue:

\[ \lambda_+ = \sigma^2 \left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{N}{T}}\right)^2 \]

Detoning step (optional): Removes the largest eigenvalue (the "market mode") to isolate sector-level correlations.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.random_matrix_theory import RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator(
        denoise=True,   # remove noise eigenvalues
        detone=False,   # keep the market factor
    ),
)

When to use: Large universes where the empirical correlation matrix is dominated by noise. Pairs well with HRP and NCO allocators.

See: López de Prado (2020) — Advances in Financial Machine Learning

docs.title: Semi-Covariance (SemiCovariance)
docs.text:
Computes covariance using only downside returns (negative returns). This targets downside risk specifically, which is more relevant for loss-averse investors than full variance.

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{semi}_{ij} = \frac{1}{T^-} \sum_{t: r_{i,t} < 0} r_{i,t} \cdot r_{j,t} \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.semi_covariance import SemiCovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=SemiCovariance(),
)

When to use: When minimizing downside risk is the primary objective. Pairs naturally with MarkowitzAllocator(MIN_VOLATILITY) for drawdown-conscious portfolios.

docs.title: Option-Implied Covariance (ImpliedCovarianceEstimator)
docs.text:
Combines forward-looking Point-in-Time (PIT) Option-Implied Volatilities (from data.features["implied_vol"], such as 30-day Model-Free Implied Volatility computed by PITOptionsMFIVTransformer) with a Ledoit-Wolf shrunk correlation matrix and the Buss & Vilkov (2012) implied correlation adjustment:

\[ \Gamma_t^{\text{imp}} = (1 - \gamma_t) \Gamma_t^{\text{hist}} + \gamma_t \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top, \qquad \hat{\Sigma}_t^{\text{imp}} = D_{\text{IV}, t} \, \Gamma_t^{\text{imp}} \, D_{\text{IV}, t} \]

When an index implied volatility index_implied_vol is supplied, \(\gamma_t\) is solved in closed form so the implied market portfolio variance matches \(\sigma_{M,\text{IV}}^2\). Enabling use_cornish_fisher_tail=True applies a Cornish-Fisher four-moment tail expansion using Bakshi-Kapadia-Madan option-implied skewness ("implied_skew") and excess kurtosis ("implied_kurtosis") to inflate standalone implied volatilities for negatively skewed or fat-tailed assets. You can also directly extract the \(N \times N\) implied correlation matrix \(\Gamma_t^{\text{imp}}\) via .estimate_correlation(data) or estimator.last_implied_correlation_.

from pyalloq_features.transformers import PITOptionsMFIVTransformer
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance import ImpliedCovarianceEstimator

data = PITOptionsMFIVTransformer(option_chain_df=chains_df).transform(data)

imp_cov = ImpliedCovarianceEstimator(
    index_implied_vol=0.22,
    correlation_window=60,
    use_cornish_fisher_tail=True,
    tail_confidence=0.95,
)
corr_imp_df = imp_cov.estimate_correlation(data)  # Direct N x N implied correlation matrix

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=imp_cov,
)

When to use: Earnings seasons, macro event windows, or regime transitions where forward-looking option surfaces price in volatility and correlation risk before historical returns react.

docs.title: Graph Reaction-Diffusion (ReactionDiffusionCovarianceEstimator)
docs.text:
Models cross-asset volatility spillover and non-linear self-excitation on a dynamic Financial Precision Graph \(\mathcal{L}_t = I - D_t^{-1/2} W_t D_t^{-1/2}\) via a coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo Reaction-Diffusion ODE system integrated via 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4):

\[ \frac{dv}{dt} = -D_v \mathcal{L}_t v - \kappa_v v + \gamma_{\text{react}} v (v - \theta_{\text{crit}})(1 - v) - \beta_u u \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance import ReactionDiffusionCovarianceEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=ReactionDiffusionCovarianceEstimator(
        diffusion_coeff=0.35,
        horizon_steps=5,
    ),
)

When to use: Sector contagion and supply-chain spillover regimes where a localized volatility shock on one asset propagates to connected neighbors ahead of trailing sample windows. Also computes last_diagnostics_ containing the Graph Laplacian's Fiedler value \(\lambda_2(\mathcal{L}_t)\), network mixing time \(\tau_{\text{mix}}\), Fiedler vector \(v_2\), and Wiener-Hopf Multivariate Hawkes branching matrix \(G = \|\Phi\|_1\) and spectral radius \(\rho(G)\).

docs.title: Deep Spatio-Temporal Graph Covariance (CRISPSparseSTGAT + DeepCovarianceEstimator)
docs.text:
Combines a continuous-time Neural Rough Differential Equation with Hawkes Jump Discontinuities (NeuralJumpRDE) at the node level with a CRISP Sparse Multi-Head Graph Attention layer and a Network-Fragility Shrinkage Cholesky Layer (FragilityShrinkageCholeskyLayer) to forecast strictly Positive Semi-Definite (PSD) covariance matrices:

from pyalloq.dl import CRISPSparseSTGAT, DeepCovarianceEstimator

stgat = CRISPSparseSTGAT(
    num_assets=len(data.assets),
    num_features=1,
    hidden_dim=32,
    num_heads=4,
    keep_ratio=0.35,
)

cov_estimator = DeepCovarianceEstimator(model=stgat, lookback_window=30)
cov_df = cov_estimator.estimate(data)

docs.title: Size- and Permutation-Equivariant Set Transformer Covariance (SetTransformerCovarianceNet)
docs.text:
Unlike lower-triangular Cholesky heads (torch.tril) whose output depends on arbitrary DataFrame column ordering, SetTransformerCovarianceNet enforces exact 2D Congruence Equivariance (\(\hat{\Sigma}(\Pi X) = \Pi \hat{\Sigma}(X) \Pi^\top\)) and zero-shot universe-size transfer via Induced Set Attention Blocks (ISAB) and Scalable-Softmax (SSMax).

It supports three pluggable PSD covariance heads:

  • head_type="factor_diag" (ISABFactorDiagonalHead, Default): Reuses the equivariant asset embeddings \(Z_t\) and invariant inducing-point factor states \(H_{I,t}\) to form \(\hat{\Sigma}_t = B_t \Sigma_{F,t} B_t^\top + D_t\). Supports exact \(\mathcal{O}(N m^2 + m^3)\) training and GMV solves via forward_factors(x, mask) and WoodburyGaussianNLLLoss / WoodburySteinLoss.
  • head_type="gram_corr" (EquivariantGramCorrHead): Volatility-scaled \(\ell_2\)-normalized Gram correlation matrix blended with learnable [REGIME] shrinkage \(\lambda_t \in (0, 1)\) and optional Point-in-Time implied-volatility anchoring.
  • head_type="rie_spectral" (RIESpectralHead): Rotation- and permutation-invariant eigenvalue cleaning inside the empirical correlation eigenbasis conditioned on the aspect ratio \(q_{\text{in}} = N_{\text{active}} / L\).
import torch
from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import RollingWindowSplitter
from pyalloq.dl import (
    DeepCovarianceEstimator,
    SetTransformerCovarianceNet,
    UniverseSubsampler,
    WoodburyGaussianNLLLoss,
)
from pyalloq.dl.trainer import WalkForwardTrainer

set_cov_net = SetTransformerCovarianceNet(
    n_features=1,
    hidden_dim=64,
    num_heads=4,
    num_inds=16,
    head_type="factor_diag",      # or "gram_corr" | "rie_spectral"
    temporal_type="vsn_conv",     # "lstm" | "vsn_conv" | "logsig_ssm" | "neural_jump_rde"
    directed_delay=True,          # Optional (t-1) causal sieve for multi-timezone closes
)

trainer = WalkForwardTrainer(
    model=set_cov_net,
    loss_function=WoodburyGaussianNLLLoss(normalize_by_cardinality=True),
    optimizer=torch.optim.AdamW(set_cov_net.parameters(), lr=2e-3),
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=120),
    lookback_window=30,
    return_mask=True,
    universe_subsampler=UniverseSubsampler(min_assets=10),
    use_forward_factors=True,     # Invokes O(Nm^2 + m^3) Woodbury pathway
)

cov_est = DeepCovarianceEstimator(model=set_cov_net, lookback_window=30, allow_ragged=True)
cov_df = cov_est.estimate(data)
factor_loadings_df, sigma_f_np, idio_var_ser = cov_est.estimate_factors(data)

docs.title: Choosing a Covariance Estimator
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Estimator Many observations, stable market EmpiricalCovariance Volatile regime, recent correlations important EWMACovariance High-dimensional, short history LedoitWolfShrinkage Large universe, correlation noise removal RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator Downside risk focus SemiCovariance Forward-looking option-implied risk & correlation ImpliedCovarianceEstimator Cross-asset network volatility spillover & contagion ReactionDiffusionCovarianceEstimator

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Covariance Estimator
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.interfaces import BaseCovarianceEstimator
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyCovariance(BaseCovarianceEstimator):
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.DataFrame:
        returns = data.prices.pct_change().dropna()
        return returns.cov() * 252

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=MyCovariance(),
)

docs.title: Data Connectors
docs.text: Data connectors fetch raw market data from external vendors and normalize it into a standardized MarketData object. All connectors inherit from BaseDataConnector.
