docs.title: Adding Features to MarketData
docs.text:
After fetching prices, attach time-series features to your MarketData:

from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData

# Fetch volume separately if your connector doesn't include it
volume_df = ...  # pd.DataFrame with same index as data.prices

enriched_data = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices,
    features={
        "volume": volume_df,
    },
    risk_free_rate=0.04,
)

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Connector
docs.text:
from pyalloq_data_connector.base import BaseDataConnector
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyDataConnector(BaseDataConnector):
    def get_market_data(
        self, tickers: list[str], start: str, end: str
    ) -> MarketData:
        # fetch from your data source
        prices = pd.DataFrame(...)
        return MarketData(prices=prices)

docs.title: Feature Engineering
docs.text: pyalloq-features provides tools to compute and attach time-series features — technical indicators, cross-sectional signals, and scaled inputs — to your MarketData. Features flow through the entire pipeline, enabling advanced estimators and ML models.

docs.title: Technical Transformers
docs.text:
Compute price-based technical indicators from MarketData.prices.

from pyalloq_features.transformers.technical import TechnicalTransformer

transformer = TechnicalTransformer()
features = transformer.transform(data)

# features is a dict[str, pd.DataFrame] ready to attach to MarketData

Available indicators include momentum, rolling volatility, RSI, and moving average crossovers. Each indicator is computed per-asset and aligned to the price index to prevent look-ahead bias.

from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData

enriched = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices,
    features=features,
)

docs.title: Cross-Sectional Transformers
docs.text:
Compute cross-sectional signals — ranking assets relative to each other at each point in time.

from pyalloq_features.transformers.cross_sectional import CrossSectionalRank

cs_transformer = CrossSectionalRank(target_feature="volume")
data = cs_transformer.transform(data)

Cross-sectional features are particularly useful with FactorReturnEstimator and custom ML-based allocators.

docs.title: Point-in-Time Option-Implied Volatility, Skewness & Kurtosis (PITOptionsMFIVTransformer)
docs.text:
Compute 30-day Model-Free Implied Volatility (MFIV) (Britten-Jones & Neuberger 2000 / CBOE VIX methodology) as well as Bakshi-Kapadia-Madan (2003) Model-Free Implied Skewness ("implied_skew") and Excess Kurtosis ("implied_kurtosis") from raw historical option chain snapshots while enforcing strict Point-in-Time (PIT) timestamp guards (quote_timestamp <= decision_timestamp) to prevent look-ahead bias.

When option chains are absent for a given asset or date, PITOptionsMFIVTransformer automatically falls back to Parkinson High-Low range volatility (if "high" and "low" exist in data.features) or EWMA realized volatility and rolling higher moments so data.features["implied_vol"], data.features["implied_skew"], and data.features["implied_kurtosis"] are always complete and aligned with data.prices.index.

from pyalloq_features.transformers import PITOptionsMFIVTransformer

pit_iv = PITOptionsMFIVTransformer(
    option_chain_df=raw_option_chains,  # optional; uses causal fallback if None
    target_horizon_days=30.0,
    market_close_offset_hours=16.0,
)
data = pit_iv.transform(data)
# Populates data.features["implied_vol"], "implied_skew", and "implied_kurtosis"

docs.title: Rough Path Log-Signatures & Lifted Heston Rough Volatility
docs.text:
To capture local non-Markovian path geometry, price-volatility lead-lag (Lévy areas), and multi-scale rough volatility without microstructure noise contamination (Cont & Das 2023), use LogSignatureTransformer and LiftedHestonRoughVolTransformer:

from pyalloq_features.transformers import (
    LiftedHestonRoughVolTransformer,
    LogSignatureTransformer,
)

# 1. Lyndon-basis truncated Log-Signatures (Level 1 increments + Level 2 Lévy areas)
data = LogSignatureTransformer(window=10, depth=2).transform(data)
# Populates: "logsig_levy_price_vol", "logsig_time_price_area", "logsig_norm"

# 2. Abi Jaber (2019) K-factor Markovian Lifted Heston Rough Volatility & Adaptive Hurst H_eff
data = LiftedHestonRoughVolTransformer(n_factors=5, estimation_window=30).transform(data)
# Populates: "lifted_heston_vol", "hurst_exponent"

docs.title: Scalers
docs.text:
Normalize features before feeding them to ML estimators or deep learning models.

from pyalloq_features.scalers import StandardFeatureScaler

scaler = StandardFeatureScaler()
scaled_features = scaler.fit_transform(features)

docs.title: Attaching Features to MarketData
docs.text:
Features must share the exact same DatetimeIndex as data.prices — MarketData.validate_alignment() enforces this at construction.

from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,
    features={
        "momentum":   momentum_df,    # time-series momentum signals
        "volume":     volume_df,      # daily volume (required by AlmgrenChriss)
        "risk_budgets": budgets_df,   # target risk allocations (for RiskBudgetingAllocator)
    },
)

docs.title: Using Features in Estimators
docs.text:
Several components read from MarketData.features:

Feature key Used by "implied_vol" ImpliedCovarianceEstimator, ReactionDiffusionCovarianceEstimator, ReactionDiffusionGenerator "risk_budgets" RiskBudgetingAllocator "volume" AlmgrenChrissCostModel Any factor data FactorReturnEstimator Any signal Custom ML estimators / DL models

docs.title: Monte Carlo Simulation & Entropy Pooling
docs.text: pyalloq-simulation provides a complete synthetic scenario engine for stress-testing portfolio strategies, expressing non-Gaussian market views via Meucci's Entropy Pooling, and running parallel multi-path walk-forward backtests across thousands of synthetic market realities.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    MD["📦 MarketData\nHistorical Prices & Features"]
    IMP["🩹 FactorBackcastImputer\nPre-IPO & Gap Imputation"]
    GEN["🎲 ScenarioGenerator\nGaussian / PCA / FHS / Copula / GMM"]
    SMD["🧊 ScenarioMarketData\n3D Tensor (M, T, N)"]
    VB["🔭 ViewBuilder & EntropyPooler\n1st & 2nd Moment Views"]
    EV["📉 ScenarioEvaluator\nCVaR, View-Adjusted MDD, Ruin"]
    PME["⚡ ParallelMonteCarloEngine\nMulti-Path WalkForwardEngine"]

    MD --> IMP --> GEN --> SMD
    SMD --> VB --> EV
    SMD --> PME

docs.title: 1. Missing Data Imputation (FactorBackcastImputer)
docs.text:
When your portfolio universe includes recent IPOs or assets with interior data gaps, a naive .dropna() truncates the entire \(N\)-asset matrix down to the shortest asset's history.

FactorBackcastImputer preserves the full historical length \(T\) by extracting principal component factors from anchor assets in return space, regressing partial-history assets onto those factors, injecting matched idiosyncratic volatility, and back-casting continuous price paths.

from pyalloq_simulation import FactorBackcastImputer

imputer = FactorBackcastImputer(
    n_components=3,
    min_coverage=0.85,
    inject_idiosyncratic_noise=True,
)
clean_data = imputer.fit_transform(raw_market_data)

Automatic Imputation in Generators

Every scenario generator enables impute_missing=True by default, automatically applying FactorBackcastImputer inside .fit(data) whenever missing observations are detected.

docs.title: 2. Scenario Generators
docs.text:
All generators implement BaseScenarioGenerator and output a ScenarioMarketData 3D tensor of shape (M, T, N) (n_paths × horizon × n_assets), along with forward-projected pd.DatetimeIndex timestamps and jointly synthesized exogenous features.

Generator Distribution & Dynamics Best Used For GaussianGenerator Multivariate Normal with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage & Cholesky factorization Fast baseline testing and isolating optimizer behavior PCAFactorGenerator \(K\) latent PCA factors + idiosyncratic Gaussian noise High-dimensional portfolios (\(N \gg K\)) FHSGenerator Univariate GARCH(1,1) filtering + synchronous empirical residual bootstrap Preserving historical volatility clustering and empirical fat tails GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) marginals + Generalized Pareto (EVT) tails + Student-\(t\) Copula Modeling extreme tail risk and simultaneous crash dependence (\(\lambda_L > 0\)) GMMRegimeGenerator \(K\)-state Gaussian Mixture Model + Markov transition matrix Stress-testing structural breaks and Bull/Bear regime shifts ReactionDiffusionGenerator Coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo Graph Reaction-Diffusion SDE + Leverage Effect on Precision Graph Laplacian Simulating cross-asset volatility spillover, network contagion, and localized shock propagation ConditionalDiffusionGenerator Factor-bottleneck score-based denoising diffusion conditioned on PIT implied_vol & Depth-2 Rough Log-Signatures + DDIM sampler Non-parametric cross-sectional trajectories capturing fat tails, skewness, and correlation breakdowns NeuralSDEGenerator Arbitrage-free coupled jump-diffusion Neural SDE with Hansen-Jagannathan Sharpe bound & Signature-MMD calibration Continuous-time multi-horizon trajectory synthesis and instantaneous covariance surfaces

docs.title: Generating Scenarios
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pyalloq_simulation import (
    ConditionalDiffusionGenerator,
    GaussianGenerator,
    PCAFactorGenerator,
    FHSGenerator,
    GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator,
    GMMRegimeGenerator,
    NeuralSDEGenerator,
    ReactionDiffusionGenerator,
)

# Example 1: GARCH-EVT-Student-t Copula Generator
generator = GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator(
    nu=5.0,
    lower_quantile=0.10,
    upper_quantile=0.90,
    dtype=np.float32,
    impute_missing=True,
)
generator.fit(data, log_returns=False)

scenario_data = generator.generate(n_paths=2000, horizon=252)
print(scenario_data.prices.shape)  # (2000, 252, N)

# Example 2: Graph Reaction-Diffusion Contagion Generator with Point Shock
rd_gen = ReactionDiffusionGenerator(diffusion_coeff=0.35, leverage_rho=-0.45)
rd_gen.fit(data)
contagion_scenarios = rd_gen.generate(
    n_paths=500,
    horizon=60,
    initial_shock={data.assets[0]: 0.80},  # Inject localized volatility shock
)

# Example 3: Factor-Based Conditional Diffusion with Fast DDIM Sampling
diff_gen = ConditionalDiffusionGenerator(
    n_factors=4,
    condition_window=15,
    ddim_steps=20,
    ddim_eta=0.25,
)
diff_scenarios = diff_gen.estimate_scenarios(data, n_paths=500, horizon=30)

# Example 4: Arbitrage-Free Neural SDE Generator
sde_gen = NeuralSDEGenerator(
    max_market_price_of_risk=1.75,
    substeps_per_day=2,
)
sde_scenarios = sde_gen.estimate_scenarios(data, n_paths=500, horizon=30)
cov_t0 = sde_gen.estimate_instantaneous_covariance()

docs.title: Memory Management & Tensor Batching
docs.text:
A \(10,000 \times 252 \times 500\) simulation in float64 consumes over 20 GB of RAM across price and return tensors. To prevent out-of-memory (OOM) spikes in cloud containers or parallel workers:

  1. Precision Control: All generators default to dtype=np.float32 (configurable to np.float64).
  2. Streamed Batch Generation: Use generate_batches() to yield memory-bounded ScenarioMarketData chunks:
for batch in generator.generate_batches(n_paths=10_000, horizon=252, batch_size=1_000):
    # Each batch holds only (1000, 252, N) in float32
    process_batch(batch)

docs.title: 3. Expressing Market Views & Entropy Pooling
docs.text: Unlike Black-Litterman—which is restricted to normal distributions and linear return views—Meucci's Entropy Pooling blends any non-Gaussian Monte Carlo prior with first-moment (return) and second-moment (volatility and correlation/covariance) views by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between prior probabilities \(p\) and posterior probabilities \(x^*\).

docs.title: Supported View Types
docs.text:
View Class Moment Example AbsoluteView 1st (Return) "AAPL cumulative return >= 5%" RelativeView 1st (Spread) "MSFT outperforms GOOGL by >= 2%" VolatilityView 2nd (Volatility) "AAPL volatility increases by 50% (multiplier=1.5)" CovarianceView 2nd (Correlation / Covariance) "AAPL–MSFT correlation >= 0.60" 
from pyalloq_simulation import (
    AbsoluteView,
    RelativeView,
    VolatilityView,
    CovarianceView,
    ViewBuilder,
    EntropyPooler,
)

views = [
    AbsoluteView(asset="AAPL", operator="==", target=0.08),
    RelativeView(asset_outperformer="MSFT", asset_underperformer="AMZN", operator=">=", target=0.02),
    VolatilityView(asset="AAPL", operator=">=", multiplier=1.50),
    CovarianceView(asset_1="AAPL", asset_2="MSFT", operator=">=", target_correlation=0.50),
]

builder = ViewBuilder(scenario_data)
A_ineq, b_ineq, C_eq, d_eq = builder.build(views)

pooler = EntropyPooler(n_scenarios=scenario_data.n_paths)
entropy_result = pooler.fit(A_ineq=A_ineq, b_ineq=b_ineq, C_eq=C_eq, d_eq=d_eq)

print(f"Converged: {entropy_result.success}, KL Divergence: {entropy_result.kl_divergence:.4f}")

docs.title: 4. Path-Dependent Risk Evaluation (ScenarioEvaluator)
docs.text:
Terminal metrics alone miss intra-horizon crashes that trigger margin calls or risk limits. ScenarioEvaluator evaluates both terminal and intra-horizon path metrics across all \(t \in [0, T]\) weighted by the posterior scenario probabilities entropy_result.weights:

  • expected_return: Posterior probability-weighted cumulative return.
  • volatility: Posterior probability-weighted return standard deviation.
  • sharpe_ratio: View-adjusted horizon Sharpe ratio.
  • cvar_95: Posterior probability-weighted 95% Conditional Value-at-Risk (Expected Shortfall).
  • view_adjusted_mdd: Posterior probability-weighted Maximum Drawdown across the \((M, T+1)\) wealth trajectory.
  • probability_of_ruin: Posterior probability mass of paths whose intra-horizon drawdown or equity drop breaches ruin_threshold (default -0.30, i.e., a 30% loss).
import numpy as np
from pyalloq_simulation import ScenarioEvaluator

evaluator = ScenarioEvaluator(risk_free_rate=0.03, ruin_threshold=-0.30)
weights = np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25])

metrics = evaluator.evaluate(
    scenario_data=scenario_data,
    asset_weights=weights,
    entropy_result=entropy_result,
)

print(f"Expected Return:     {metrics.expected_return:.2%}")
print(f"CVaR (95%):          {metrics.cvar_95:.2%}")
print(f"View-Adjusted MDD:   {metrics.view_adjusted_mdd:.2%}")
print(f"Probability of Ruin: {metrics.probability_of_ruin:.2%}")

docs.title: 5. Multi-Path Strategy Backtesting (ParallelMonteCarloEngine)
docs.text: To evaluate how a full StrategyPipeline and WalkForwardEngine perform across hundreds or thousands of synthetic market paths, use ParallelMonteCarloEngine (also aliased as MonteCarloEngine in pyalloq_core.engines).

docs.title: Hybrid Feature Synthesis for Deep Learning & Technical Indicators
docs.text:
1. Exogenous Features (data.features): Automatically projected inside every BaseScenarioGenerator conditioned on simulated asset returns so Deep Learning estimators (such as DeepCovarianceEstimator) receive aligned 3D feature tensors.
  2. Endogenous Technical Features (FeaturePipeline): Pass a FeaturePipeline to ParallelMonteCarloEngine(feature_pipeline=...) to deterministically recompute price-derived indicators (e.g., RSI, MACD, rolling volatility) on each synthetic path inside the worker pool.
from pyalloq_core.engines import ParallelMonteCarloEngine
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine
from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import RollingWindowSplitter
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator
from pyalloq_features.core.pipeline import FeaturePipeline
from pyalloq_simulation import GaussianGenerator

# 1. Fit generator on historical MarketData
gen = GaussianGenerator()
gen.fit(data)

# 2. Configure standard WalkForwardEngine
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets))
wf_engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=60),
    rebalance_freq="ME",
)

# 3. Execute across streamed scenario batches in parallel
mc_engine = ParallelMonteCarloEngine(
    backtest_engine=wf_engine,
    max_workers=4,
    feature_pipeline=FeaturePipeline(),  # optional per-path feature transformers
)

batches = gen.generate_batches(n_paths=100, horizon=252, batch_size=25)
mc_result = mc_engine.run_batches(batches)

print(mc_result.equity_curves.shape)          # (T, 100)
print(mc_result.metrics_distribution.head())  # Distribution of Sharpe, MDD, Sortino across paths

docs.title: Multi-Period Portfolio Optimization (MPO) — User Guide
docs.text: PyAlloq provides a complete, modular suite of Multi-Period Portfolio Optimization (MPO) estimators, allocators, differentiable neural layers, and reinforcement learning environments that seamlessly plug into StrategyPipeline and WalkForwardEngine.

docs.title: How Stateful Rebalancing Works in WalkForwardEngine
docs.text:
In multi-period optimization, the optimal trade at date \(t\) depends on your current drifted holdings \(w_{t^-}\) immediately prior to rebalancing.

  • WalkForwardEngine automatically tracks intra-period asset price drift and passes current_weights=w_{t^-} into StrategyPipeline.generate_weights(..., current_weights=current_w_series) on every rebalance date.
  • Single-period allocators ignore current_weights, while multi-period allocators use current_weights to penalize turnover, model market impact, and return a MultiPeriodOptimizationResult containing both the immediate trade execution result.weights and the planned \(H\)-stage trajectory result.weights_trajectory.

docs.title: Pillar 1: Classical Convex MPC, ADMM & Stochastic MPC
1. Multi-Horizon Alpha Decay + Boyd/Gârleanu-Pedersen MPC
docs.text:
Combine AlphaDecayReturnEstimator with MultiPeriodMPCAllocator:

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfCovariance
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.multi_horizon import AlphaDecayReturnEstimator
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.multi_period import MultiPeriodMPCAllocator
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import FlatBpsCostModel
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline

# 1. Multi-horizon return estimator with fast (5d), medium (21d), and slow (63d) half-lives
return_estimator = AlphaDecayReturnEstimator(
    horizon=5,
    half_lives=(5.0, 21.0, 63.0),
)

# 2. Boyd (2017) + Garleanu-Pedersen (2013) Convex MPC Allocator
mpc_allocator = MultiPeriodMPCAllocator(
    horizon=5,
    risk_aversion=3.0,
    spread_cost_bps=10.0,       # p=1 proportional bid-ask spread (no-trade zone)
    impact_coeff=0.05,          # p=3/2 square-root market impact cone
    quad_cost_coeff=0.01,       # p=2 temporary quadratic cost
    permanent_impact_eta=0.02,  # Garleanu-Pedersen permanent impact
    permanent_impact_rho=0.3,   # Market resilience decay rate
    max_turnover_per_stage=0.40,
    backend="cvxpy",            # Use "admm" for fast operator splitting
)

# Inspect a single H-stage trajectory directly
res = mpc_allocator.allocate(
    data=market_data,
    cov_matrix=LedoitWolfCovariance().estimate(market_data),
    expected_returns=return_estimator.estimate_trajectory(market_data),
)
print("Immediate Execution Weights (t+0):\n", res.weights)
print("Planned 5-Stage Trajectory:\n", res.weights_trajectory)

# Or run a full stateful Walk-Forward Backtest
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=mpc_allocator,
    return_estimator=return_estimator,
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfCovariance(),
)
engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="W-FRI",
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(bps=10.0),
)
bt_result = engine.run(market_data)

docs.title: 2. Fast Operator Splitting (backend="admm")
docs.text:
When running large hyperparameter sweeps or large asset universes without solver overhead, switch backend="admm":

admm_allocator = MultiPeriodMPCAllocator(
    horizon=5,
    risk_aversion=3.0,
    spread_cost_bps=10.0,
    quad_cost_coeff=0.02,
    backend="admm",
    admm_max_iter=200,
)

docs.title: 3. Scenario-Tree Stochastic MPC with CVaR Tail Control
docs.text:
Optimize over Monte Carlo or Entropy-Pooled scenario tensors (ScenarioMarketData):

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.stochastic_mpc import StochasticScenarioMPCAllocator
from pyalloq_simulation.generators.gaussian import GaussianGenerator

gen = GaussianGenerator()
gen.fit(market_data)
scenarios = gen.generate(n_scenarios=250, horizon=5)

stoch_mpc = StochasticScenarioMPCAllocator(
    cvar_alpha=0.95,
    cvar_weight=2.0,
    spread_cost_bps=10.0,
)
stoch_res = stoch_mpc.allocate(scenarios)

docs.title: Pillar 2: Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) & IPMO
docs.text:
Use MultiHorizonPredictorNet, MDFPOptimizationLayer, HybridDFLLoss, and IPMOAllocator to train neural predictors end-to-end through the multi-period fixed-point optimization layer:

import torch
from pyalloq.dl.estimators.e2e.ipmo_allocator import IPMOAllocator, MultiHorizonPredictorNet
from pyalloq.dl.layers.mdfp import MDFPOptimizationLayer
from pyalloq.dl.loss_functions.dfl import HybridDFLLoss

n_assets = len(market_data.assets)
predictor = MultiHorizonPredictorNet(n_assets=n_assets, n_features=1, horizon=5)
mdfp_layer = MDFPOptimizationLayer(
    horizon=5,
    risk_aversion=2.5,
    cost_penalty=0.001,
    implicit_backward=True,  # O(1) memory implicit differentiation via Neumann VJPs
)
loss_fn = HybridDFLLoss(alpha=0.7, cost_penalty=0.001, risk_aversion=2.5)

# Wrap in IPMOAllocator for StrategyPipeline / WalkForwardEngine execution
ipmo_allocator = IPMOAllocator(
    predictor=predictor,
    mdfp_layer=mdfp_layer,
    lookback_window=30,
)

docs.title: Pillar 3: FinRL DRL, RL-BHRP, Deep Hedging & Thermodynamic Gates
1. Two-Level Bayesian HRP (BayesianHRPAllocator)
docs.text:
from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.bhrp import BayesianHRPAllocator

bhrp = BayesianHRPAllocator(
    tau=0.3,
    return_tilt_strength=2.0,
    turnover_penalty=0.5,
)

docs.title: 2. Deep Hedging Trajectory Policy + Thermodynamic Regime Gate
docs.text:
from pyalloq.rl import (
    DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer,
    RLAllocator,
    TrajectoryPolicyNet,
    WassersteinRegimeGate,
)

policy = TrajectoryPolicyNet(n_assets=len(market_data.assets), lookback_window=20)
trainer = DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer(
    policy=policy,
    horizon=5,
    transaction_cost_bps=10.0,
    risk_aversion=2.0,
)
trainer.fit_on_market_data(market_data, epochs=15)

regime_gate = WassersteinRegimeGate(fast_window=15, slow_window=45, w2_threshold=0.025)
rl_allocator = RLAllocator(
    policy=policy,
    lookback_window=20,
    regime_gate=regime_gate,
)

docs.title: Visualizing Multi-Period Optimization with pyalloq-viz
docs.text:
pyalloq-viz provides dedicated interactive Plotly charts and MultiPeriodTearSheet for multi-period trajectories, alpha decay surfaces, thermodynamic regime gates, and cross-pillar net-of-cost comparisons:

from pyalloq_viz import (
    MultiPeriodTearSheet,
    plot_alpha_decay_surface,
    plot_mpc_trajectory,
    plot_mpo_pillar_comparison,
    plot_thermodynamic_regime_gate,
)

# 1. Individual interactive figures
fig_traj = plot_mpc_trajectory(res, current_weights=current_w)
fig_decay = plot_alpha_decay_surface(return_estimator.estimate_horizon(market_data))
fig_gate = plot_thermodynamic_regime_gate(market_data, fast_window=15, slow_window=45)
fig_bench = plot_mpo_pillar_comparison({"MPC": bt_result})

# 2. Standalone HTML Tear Sheet Dashboard
ts = MultiPeriodTearSheet(
    mpo_result=res,
    horizon_forecasts=return_estimator.estimate_horizon(market_data),
    market_data=market_data,
    strategy_comparison={"MPC": bt_result},
)
ts.to_html("visualizations_output/mpo/multi_period_tearsheet.html")

docs.title: Institutional Reinforcement Learning (pyalloq[rl])
docs.text: pyalloq[rl] provides an institutional Reinforcement Learning ecosystem that strictly decouples your feature engineering pipeline (pyalloq-features) from continuous-control environments (POMDPPortfolioEnv, MetaPortfolioEnv), non-linear market impact models (AlmgrenChrissCostModel), online risk-adjusted rewards, and policy training (SB3PortfolioAgent, DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer, HierarchicalMetaRLAllocator).

docs.title: 1. Evolvable State Spaces (spaces.Dict & DictFlattenWrapper)
docs.text:
To allow your RL agent to ingest technical indicators today and MiniRocket or TimesFM embeddings tomorrow without rewriting the environment, POMDPPortfolioEnv emits a 3-key gymnasium.spaces.Dict observation:

Dictionary Key Shape Description "market_state" (lookback_window, n_assets, n_features) Dynamically sized 3D feature tensor (channel 0 is simple returns; channels 1..F-1 are FeaturePipeline outputs). "current_weights" (n_assets,) Previous step's drifted risky portfolio weights \(w_{t-1}\). "portfolio_meta" (3,) Internal friction & regime meta-state: [unrealized_drawdown, cash_reserve, w2_distance].

When connecting to standard Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) policies in stable-baselines3, DictFlattenWrapper automatically flattens this spaces.Dict into a single 1D spaces.Box vector and provides .unflatten(flat_obs) to reconstruct the 3D tensor structure for custom Spatio-Temporal Attention extractors.

from pyalloq_features.core.pipeline import FeaturePipeline
from pyalloq_features.transformers.technical import TechnicalIndicator
from pyalloq.rl import POMDPPortfolioEnv, DictFlattenWrapper, FeatureNormalizationWrapper

feature_pipeline = FeaturePipeline().add(
    TechnicalIndicator("RSI", timeperiod=14)
)

env = POMDPPortfolioEnv(
    scenario_data=scenario_data,       # 3D (M, T, N) ScenarioMarketData
    feature_pipeline=feature_pipeline, # Lazily evaluated & cached per sampled path
    lookback_window=20,
    include_cash=True,
    projection_mode="softmax",         # "softmax", "dirichlet", or "relu_l1"
)

# Normalize rolling features and flatten for MLP policies
wrapped_env = DictFlattenWrapper(FeatureNormalizationWrapper(env))

docs.title: 2. The Multiverse POMDP Environment (POMDPPortfolioEnv)
docs.text:
Historical financial series only provide a single realization of the past. POMDPPortfolioEnv ingests a 3D ScenarioMarketData cube \((M, T, N)\) generated by pyalloq-simulation (such as GMMRegimeGenerator or GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator):

  • Synthetic Path Spawning: On every reset(), the agent is spawned into a randomly sampled trajectory \(m \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}\), preventing overfitting to a single historical timeline.
  • Lazy Feature Caching: If a FeaturePipeline is attached, scenario_data.get_path(m, feature_pipeline=...) is computed on-demand when trajectory \(m\) is first visited and cached in memory.
  • Simplex Action Projection: Continuous policy outputs \(a_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}\) are projected onto the long-only simplex \(\Delta^{N+1}\) via "softmax", "dirichlet" (concentration sampling during stochastic exploration), or "relu_l1".

docs.title: Pluggable Cost Models (BaseCostModel)
docs.text: POMDPPortfolioEnv accepts any pyalloq_backtest.costs.BaseCostModel instance—including FlatBpsCostModel, ProportionalSpreadCostModel, and AlmgrenChrissCostModel (non-linear square-root market impact)—and deducts execution costs directly from the step return before passing \(r_{p,t}^{\text{net}}\) to the reward function.

docs.title: Online Reward Functions (pyalloq.rl.rewards)
docs.text:
• DifferentialSharpeReward: Moody & Saffell (2001) online Differential Sharpe Ratio: $\(D_t = \frac{B_{t-1} \Delta A_t - \frac{1}{2} A_{t-1} \Delta B_t}{(B_{t-1} - A_{t-1}^2)^{3/2}}\)$
  • StepwiseSortinoReward: Rolling step-wise excess return divided by downside semi-deviation below a target MAR.
  • CARAUtilReward: Log-wealth Constant Absolute Risk Aversion (CARA) utility with quadratic variance, drawdown, and Bures-Wasserstein \(W_2\) turnover penalties.

docs.title: 4. Continuous Control Agents (SB3PortfolioAgent)
docs.text:
SB3PortfolioAgent orchestrates continuous-control algorithms ("PPO", "SAC", "DDPG", "TD3", "A2C"). When stable-baselines3 is installed (uv sync --extra rl), it delegates directly to SB3 over DictFlattenWrapper(env). In lightweight environments without SB3, it transparently falls back to a built-in PyTorch Actor-Critic PPO implementation.

from pyalloq_backtest.costs import AlmgrenChrissCostModel
from pyalloq.rl import (
    POMDPPortfolioEnv,
    DifferentialSharpeReward,
    SB3PortfolioAgent,
    RLAllocator,
)

env = POMDPPortfolioEnv(
    scenario_data=scenario_data,
    lookback_window=20,
    cost_model=AlmgrenChrissCostModel(portfolio_aum=1e6, spread_bps=2.0, gamma=0.05),
    reward_function=DifferentialSharpeReward(eta=0.02),
    include_cash=True,
)

agent = SB3PortfolioAgent(env=env, algorithm="PPO", hidden_dim=64)
agent.fit(total_timesteps=10_000)

# Wrap as a standard PyAlloq BaseAllocator for WalkForwardEngine
allocator = RLAllocator(
    policy=agent,
    lookback_window=20,
    use_pomdp_obs=True,
    include_cash=True,
)

docs.title: 5. Hierarchical Meta-RL (HierarchicalMetaRLAllocator)
docs.text:
Instead of forcing an RL policy to pick raw individual asset weights across noisy universes, HierarchicalMetaRLAllocator operates as a high-level Capital Allocation Committee:

  1. Level 1 (Base Allocators): A sequence of domain-specific BaseAllocator experts (e.g., MarkowitzAllocator, RiskParityAllocator, HRPAllocator, MultiPeriodMPCAllocator) each propose candidate weight vectors \(\mathbf{w}^{(1)}_t, \dots, \mathbf{w}^{(K)}_t \in \Delta^N\).
  2. Level 2 (Meta-Agent): Observes the Bures-Wasserstein regime shift distance \(W_2(\mathcal{N}_t, \mathcal{N}_{t-1})\), Carnot thermodynamic efficiency, and candidate allocator proposals, and outputs simplex blending coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_t \in \Delta^K\): $\(\mathbf{w}_t^{\text{final}} = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{k,t} \mathbf{w}^{(k)}_t\)$
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.markowitz import MarkowitzAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator
from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.hrp import HRPAllocator
from pyalloq.rl import MetaPortfolioEnv, SB3PortfolioAgent, HierarchicalMetaRLAllocator

base_allocators = [
    MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=tickers),
    RiskParityAllocator(tickers=tickers),
    HRPAllocator(tickers=tickers),
]

meta_env = MetaPortfolioEnv(
    scenario_data=train_data,
    base_allocators=base_allocators,
    lookback_window=30,
    rebalance_stride=10,
)

meta_agent = SB3PortfolioAgent(env=meta_env, algorithm="PPO", hidden_dim=32)
meta_agent.fit(total_timesteps=2_000)

meta_allocator = HierarchicalMetaRLAllocator(
    base_allocators=base_allocators,
    meta_agent=meta_agent,
    lookback_window=30,
    tickers=tickers,
)

docs.title: 6. Differentiable KKT Classical Layers & Endogenous Liquidity Impact Wrapper
Differentiable Risk Parity & CVaR KKT Layers (pyalloq.dl.layers)
docs.text:
To embed classical convex Risk Parity (DifferentiableRiskParityLayer) or Rockafellar-Uryasev CVaR (DifferentiableCVaRLayer) inside an end-to-end differentiable PyTorch pipeline alongside CRISPSparseSTGAT, use the implicit KKT differentiation layers:

import torch
from pyalloq.dl import (
    CRISPSparseSTGAT,
    DifferentiableCVaRLayer,
    DifferentiableRiskParityLayer,
)

model = CRISPSparseSTGAT(num_assets=4, num_features=1, hidden_dim=16)
rp_layer = DifferentiableRiskParityLayer(max_iter=25)
cvar_layer = DifferentiableCVaRLayer(beta=0.95, max_iter=30)

x_batch = torch.randn(8, 20, 4, 1)
mu, cov, sparse_adj = model.predict_returns_and_cov(x_batch)

weights_rp = rp_layer(cov)          # Exact KKT Jacobian: J_y = Sigma + diag(b / (y*)^2)
weights_cvar = cvar_layer(mu, cov)  # O(1)-memory Implicit Function Theorem backprop

docs.title: Endogenous Liquidity & Graph Contagion Impact Wrapper (EndogenousLiquidityImpactWrapper)
docs.text:
Wraps PortfolioGymEnv, ScenarioPortfolioEnv, or POMDPPortfolioEnv to maintain a transient order-book impact state \(q_t \in \mathbb{R}^N\) with cross-asset spillover across the normalized Graph Laplacian:

from pyalloq.rl import EndogenousLiquidityImpactWrapper, PortfolioGymEnv

env = EndogenousLiquidityImpactWrapper(
    PortfolioGymEnv(data, lookback_window=20),
    impact_lambda=0.005,
    resilience_rho=0.65,
    diffusion_kappa=0.002,
)
obs, info = env.reset(seed=42)

docs.title: 7. Unified 3-Stage E2E Policy Pipeline (BasePolicyNetwork & UnifiedE2EPolicyNetwork)
docs.text:
BasePolicyNetwork standardizes the neural controller contract forward(x, w_current=None) -> w_target across Decision-Focused Learning (DeepAllocator), pathwise Deep Hedging (DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer), and Gymnasium environments (POMDPPortfolioEnv via .predict_from_obs(obs)).

UnifiedE2EPolicyNetwork implements the 3-stage controller:

  1. Stage 1 (Perception): CRISPSparseSTGAT + LogSigSSMBlock selective state-space encoding + compute_von_neumann_entropy covariance regularity.
  2. Stage 2 (Decision / Optimization Layer): Pluggable head_mode ("mdfp", "risk_parity_kkt", "cvar_kkt", or "residual_actor").
  3. Stage 3 (Turnover-Aware No-Trade Zone): Smoothly blends KKT allocations with pre-trade weights w_current.
from pyalloq.dl import UnifiedE2EPolicyNetwork
from pyalloq.rl import DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer, POMDPPortfolioEnv, SignatureMMDRegimeGate

policy = UnifiedE2EPolicyNetwork(
    num_assets=len(data.assets),
    num_features=1,
    hidden_dim=32,
    head_mode="mdfp",
    no_trade_buffer=0.15,
)

# Train pathwise with DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer or evaluate directly on POMDPPortfolioEnv
trainer = DeepHedgingTrajectoryTrainer(policy=policy, horizon=5, lookback_window=20)
trainer.fit_on_market_data(data, epochs=10)

# Gate rebalancing turnover on rough-path Signature-MMD regime shifts
sig_gate = SignatureMMDRegimeGate(subpath_window=8, fast_window=20, slow_window=60)
diag = sig_gate.evaluate(data.prices.pct_change().dropna())

docs.title: Return Estimators
docs.text:
Return estimators produce a pd.Series of annualized expected returns — one per asset — given a MarketData object. The result is consumed by StrategyPipeline and passed to the allocator.

All estimators implement BaseReturnEstimator:

class BaseReturnEstimator(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.Series:
        ...

docs.title: Mean Historical Return (MeanHistoricalReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Computes annualized expected returns from historical price series using either the arithmetic mean (compounding=False) or geometric / CAGR mean (compounding=True), with configurable DataFrequency ("DAILY", "WEEKLY", "MONTHLY", "CRYPTO_DAILY"):

\[ \hat{\mu}_{\text{arith}} = \frac{f}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T r_t, \qquad \hat{\mu}_{\text{CAGR}} = \left(\prod_{t=1}^T (1 + r_t)\right)^{f/T} - 1 \] 
from pyalloq import MeanHistoricalReturnEstimator

# Geometric (CAGR) historical return
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=MeanHistoricalReturnEstimator(compounding=True, frequency="DAILY"),
)

docs.title: EWMA (EWMAReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Exponentially Weighted Moving Average returns. Recent observations receive higher weight. The default estimator in StrategyPipeline.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.ewma import EWMAReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=EWMAReturnEstimator(span=60),  # 60-day span
)

When to use: When you believe recent performance is more predictive than long-run historical averages.

docs.title: James-Stein (JamesSteinReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Shrinks historical mean returns towards the grand cross-sectional mean. Reduces estimation error in high-dimensional settings. Optimal for universes with \(N \geq 3\) assets.

\[ \hat{\mu}^{JS} = (1 - w) \hat{\mu} + w \bar{\mu} \mathbf{1} \]

where the shrinkage intensity \(w\) is:

\[ w = \min\left(1, \frac{N-2}{(\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})}\right) \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
)

When to use: Large universes (10+ assets) where sample mean is noisy and you want a theoretically grounded shrinkage.

docs.title: Volatility-Scaled Multi-Horizon Momentum (VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator)
docs.text:
Computes raw momentum over multiple lookback horizons (by default 63, 126, and 252 trading days, skipping the most recent 21 days to avoid 1-month short-term reversal). Each horizon return is normalized by realized volatility, and the resulting scores are standardized cross-sectionally to produce stable relative return forecasts.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator(
        horizons=(63, 126, 252),
        skip_period=21,
    ),
)

When to use: Equity or multi-asset universes where momentum signals across varying horizons need to be aggregated and risk-adjusted without letting high-volatility assets dominate.

docs.title: Residual Momentum (ResidualMomentumEstimator)
docs.text:
Isolates idiosyncratic price momentum by regressing each asset's historical returns on a cross-sectional market proxy to remove systemic market beta:

\[ R_{i, t} = \alpha_i + \beta_i R_{m, t} + \epsilon_{i, t} \]

Standardized cumulative residuals \(\sum \epsilon_{i, t} / \sigma_{\epsilon, i}\) are then converted to cross-sectional Z-scores.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import ResidualMomentumEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=ResidualMomentumEstimator(
        lookback=252,
        skip_period=21,
    ),
)

When to use: You want trend-following exposure driven purely by asset-specific performance rather than co-movement with broader equity indices.

docs.title: Factor Returns (MultiFactorReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Estimates expected returns using a factor model. Asset returns are attributed to systematic risk factors (e.g., Fama-French). The factor loadings are estimated from data.features.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.factor import MultiFactorReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=MultiFactorReturnEstimator(),
)

When to use: You have factor data attached to MarketData.features and want a structured return model.

docs.title: Implied Returns (ImpliedReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Reverse-engineers expected returns from observed market-capitalization weights using the Black-Litterman equilibrium formula:

\[ \Pi = \lambda \Sigma w^{mkt} \]

where \(\lambda\) is the implied risk aversion from the market, \(\Sigma\) is the covariance matrix, and \(w^{mkt}\) are cap-weighted market weights.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.implied import ImpliedReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=ImpliedReturnEstimator(),
)

When to use: You want returns that are consistent with market equilibrium, as a neutral starting point before overlaying views.

docs.title: Variance & Skewness Risk Premium (VarianceRiskPremiumEstimator)
docs.text:
Estimates expected excess asset returns from the Point-in-Time Variance Risk Premium (VRP) (Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou 2009) and the Bakshi-Kapadia-Madan (2003) Crash-Skewness Risk Premium:

\[ \text{VRP}_{i,t} = \sigma_{i,t,\text{IV}}^2 - \sigma_{i,t,\text{RV}}^2, \qquad \hat{\mu}_{i,t} = r_f + \gamma_{\text{vrp}} \text{VRP}_{i,t} + \eta_{\text{skew}} (-\text{MFIS}_{i,t}) \sigma_{i,t,\text{IV}} \]

When data.features["implied_vol"], data.features["lifted_heston_vol"], and data.features["implied_skew"] are populated by PITOptionsMFIVTransformer and LiftedHestonRoughVolTransformer, VarianceRiskPremiumEstimator uses them directly; otherwise it falls back to causal realized equivalents.

from pyalloq import VarianceRiskPremiumEstimator, StrategyPipeline

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=VarianceRiskPremiumEstimator(
        vrp_aversion=1.5,
        skew_aversion=0.08,
        realized_window=30,
    ),
)

docs.title: Black-Litterman (BlackLittermanEstimator)
docs.text:
Blends the market equilibrium returns \(\Pi\) with investor views \(Q\) expressed through a picking matrix \(P\). Returns both a posterior expected return vector and a posterior covariance matrix.

\[ \mu^* = \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top \Omega^{-1} P\right]^{-1} \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} \Pi + P^\top \Omega^{-1} Q\right] \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.black_litterman.bayesian import BlackLittermanEstimator
import pandas as pd

# Define views: "AAPL will outperform MSFT by 5%"
P = pd.DataFrame([[1, -1, 0]], columns=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"])
Q = pd.DataFrame([[0.05]])

bl = BlackLittermanEstimator(tau=0.05, risk_aversion=2.5)
mu_bl, cov_bl = bl.estimate(
    market_caps=market_caps,
    cov_matrix=cov_matrix,
    P=P,
    Q=Q,
)

Using Black-Litterman directly inside StrategyPipeline

Use BlackLittermanReturnEstimator (BaseReturnEstimator) and BlackLittermanCovarianceEstimator (BaseCovarianceEstimator) to plug Black-Litterman directly into StrategyPipeline and WalkForwardEngine:

from pyalloq import (
    BlackLittermanCovarianceEstimator,
    BlackLittermanReturnEstimator,
    MarkowitzAllocator,
    StrategyPipeline,
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    returns_estimator=BlackLittermanReturnEstimator(P=P, Q=Q, tau=0.05),
    cov_estimator=BlackLittermanCovarianceEstimator(P=P, Q=Q, tau=0.05),
)

docs.title: Deep Learning / Foundation Models: TimesFM 3.0
docs.text:
Google's TimesFM 3.0 is a pretrained foundation model for zero-shot time-series forecasting. PyAlloq integrates TimesFM 3.0 for both point return estimation and probabilistic view generation for Black-Litterman.

Installation requirement

TimesFM integration requires the deep learning optional dependency: 

uv add pyalloq[dl]
# or pip install "pyalloq[dl]"

docs.title: Zero-Shot Return Estimation
docs.text:
PyAlloq provides both univariate and multivariate return estimators based on TimesFM 3.0:

  • TimesFM3UnivariateReturnEstimator: Forecasts each asset series independently.
  • TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator: Forecasts cross-asset relationships jointly and optionally ingests past and future covariates from MarketData.features and MarketData.future_features.

For a forecast horizon \(H\) (in trading days) and forecasted price \(\hat{P}_{T+H, i}\), expected returns are annualized:

\[ \hat{\mu}_i = \left(\frac{\hat{P}_{T+H, i}}{P_{T, i}} - 1\right) \times \frac{252}{H} \] 
from pyalloq.dl.estimators.returns.timesfm import (
    TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator,
    TimesFM3UnivariateReturnEstimator,
)
from timesfm3 import TimesFM3Evaluator

# Initialize the TimesFM 3.0 evaluator
tfm = TimesFM3Evaluator.load_pretrained(...)

# 1. Univariate return estimator (forecasts assets independently)
univariate_est = TimesFM3UnivariateReturnEstimator(model=tfm, horizon=21)

# 2. Multivariate return estimator (leverages cross-asset dynamics & features)
multivariate_est = TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator(
    model=tfm, horizon=21, annualize=True
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=multivariate_est,
)

When to use: Zero-shot price forecasting across regimes without needing to train or fine-tune neural networks locally. Multivariate mode is ideal when macro/factor features or cross-asset dependencies exist.

docs.title: TimesFM 3.0 Black-Litterman View Generation
docs.text:
Black-Litterman typically requires subjective investor views (\(Q\)) and a diagonal confidence/uncertainty matrix (\(\Omega\)). TimesFM 3.0 natively outputs probabilistic forecast quantiles (\(p_{10}, p_{50}, p_{90}\)), which PyAlloq turns into objective, probabilistic views:

  1. View Vector (\(Q\)): The median forecast \(p_{50}\) defines the expected return view for each asset: [ Q_i = \left(\frac{p_{50, i}}{P_{T, i}} - 1\right) \times \frac{252}{H} ]
  2. Uncertainty Matrix (\(\Omega\)): Under a Gaussian assumption, the 80% credible interval (\(p_{10}\) to \(p_{90}\)) corresponds to \(2 \times 1.28 \approx 2.56\) standard deviations. The annualized forecast standard deviation is: [ \sigma_{i} = \frac{p_{90, i} - p_{10, i}}{2.56 \cdot P_{T, i}} \times \sqrt{\frac{252}{H}} ] The uncertainty matrix \(\Omega\) is the diagonal matrix of these view variances: [ \Omega = \operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2, \ldots, \sigma_N^2\right) ]
  3. Picking Matrix (\(P\)): Identity matrix \(I_N\), since views are generated for all assets.
from pyalloq.dl.estimators.black_litterman.timesfm import (
    TimesFM3MultivariateViewGenerator,
    TimesFM3UnivariateViewGenerator,
)
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.black_litterman.bayesian import BlackLittermanEstimator
from timesfm3 import TimesFM3Evaluator

tfm = TimesFM3Evaluator.load_pretrained(...)

# Generate objective views and uncertainty directly from TimesFM quantiles
view_generator = TimesFM3MultivariateViewGenerator(model=tfm, horizon=21)
P, Q, Omega = view_generator.generate(market_data)

# Blend with market equilibrium in Black-Litterman
bl = BlackLittermanEstimator(tau=0.05, risk_aversion=2.5)
mu_bl, cov_bl = bl.estimate(
    market_caps=market_data.cross_sectional,
    cov_matrix=cov_matrix,
    P=P,
    Q=Q,
)

When to use: You want Black-Litterman portfolio optimization but want systematic, probabilistic foundation model forecasts to drive the views and quantify view uncertainty.

docs.title: Deep Learning / Foundation Models: Mistral Timestral
docs.text:
Mistral AI's Timestral (mistralai/Timestral-5M, Timestral-28M, Timestral-123M, Timestral-209M) is a family of open-source time-series foundation models built on Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF) that supports up to 32,768 historical time steps and outputs 21 non-crossing quantiles (0.01 to 0.99) per forecast step on CPU or GPU.

Installation requirement

Install the deep learning extra along with the standalone timestral package: 

uv add "pyalloq[dl]"
pip install git+https://github.com/mistralai/timestral.git

docs.title: Zero-Shot Return Estimation with Timestral
docs.text:
PyAlloq provides both univariate and multivariate return estimators powered by TimestralForecaster:

  • TimestralUnivariateReturnEstimator: Forecasts each asset series independently as a 3D batch (N_assets, 1, T).
  • TimestralMultivariateReturnEstimator: Forecasts all assets jointly (1, N_assets, T) while incorporating both past-only covariates (MarketData.features \(\to\) past_covariates) and known-future covariates (MarketData.future_features \(\to\) known_covariates).

Both classes accept either a pre-loaded TimestralForecaster instance or a Hugging Face model ID string (defaulting to lazy-loading "mistralai/Timestral-28M" on first call).

from pyalloq.dl import (
    TimestralMultivariateReturnEstimator,
    TimestralUnivariateReturnEstimator,
)
from timestral import TimestralForecaster

# Option A: Pass a pre-loaded TimestralForecaster
forecaster = TimestralForecaster.from_pretrained("mistralai/Timestral-209M", device="cpu")
univariate_est = TimestralUnivariateReturnEstimator(model=forecaster, horizon=21)

# Option B: Lazy-load directly by Hugging Face checkpoint ID
multivariate_est = TimestralMultivariateReturnEstimator(
    model="mistralai/Timestral-28M",
    horizon=21,
    annualize=True,
    device="cpu",
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=multivariate_est,
)

docs.title: Timestral Black-Litterman View Generation (21 Quantiles)
docs.text:
Because Timestral outputs 21 calibrated quantiles (0.01 through 0.99), TimestralUnivariateViewGenerator and TimestralMultivariateViewGenerator allow customizing the confidence_interval=(q_low, q_high) (default (0.10, 0.90)):

  1. View Vector (\(Q\)): Computed from the median trajectory forecast.median: [ Q_i = \left(\frac{p_{50, i}}{P_{T, i}} - 1\right) \times \frac{252}{H} ]
  2. Uncertainty Matrix (\(\Omega\)): For any chosen quantile pair \((q_{\text{low}}, q_{\text{high}})\), the Gaussian z-score spread \(\Delta z = \Phi^{-1}(q_{\text{high}}) - \Phi^{-1}(q_{\text{low}})\) (which equals \(2.56\) for \((0.10, 0.90)\)) converts the inter-quantile price spread into an annualized return variance: [ \sigma_i = \frac{Q_{q_{\text{high}}, i} - Q_{q_{\text{low}}, i}}{\Delta z \cdot P_{T, i}} \times \sqrt{\frac{252}{H}}, \qquad \Omega = \operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_1^2, \ldots, \sigma_N^2\right) ]
from pyalloq.dl import (
    TimestralMultivariateViewGenerator,
    TimestralUnivariateViewGenerator,
)
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.black_litterman.bayesian import BlackLittermanEstimator

# Generate views and uncertainty using Timestral's 5th-to-95th percentile spread
view_generator = TimestralMultivariateViewGenerator(
    model="mistralai/Timestral-28M",
    horizon=21,
    confidence_interval=(0.05, 0.95),
)
P, Q, Omega = view_generator.generate(market_data)

bl = BlackLittermanEstimator(tau=0.05, risk_aversion=2.5)
mu_bl, cov_bl = bl.estimate(
    market_caps=market_data.cross_sectional,
    cov_matrix=cov_matrix,
    P=P,
    Q=Q,
    Omega=Omega,
)

docs.title: Arbitrage-Free Neural SDE (NeuralSDEEstimator)
docs.text:
NeuralSDEEstimator is a dual-role continuous-time generative estimator that calibrates a coupled price-volatility jump-diffusion Neural SDE (ArbitrageFreeNeuralSDENet) using Cholesky transition likelihood, a Hansen-Jagannathan market-price-of-risk bound (\(\|\theta_t\|_2 \le \theta_{\max}\)), and differentiable Depth-2 Rough Log-Signature MMD.

It supports:

  1. Forward Return Estimation (BaseReturnEstimator): .estimate(data) returns annualized expected returns integrated over horizon.
  2. 3D Trajectory Synthesis (BaseScenarioEstimator): .estimate_scenarios(data, n_paths, horizon) returns a 3D ScenarioMarketData tensor.
  3. Instantaneous & Horizon Covariance Surfaces: .estimate_covariance(data) and .estimate_instantaneous_covariance(data) return strictly PSD \(N \times N\) covariance DataFrames.
from pyalloq.dl import NeuralSDEEstimator

sde_estimator = NeuralSDEEstimator(
    horizon=20,
    n_paths=250,
    max_market_price_of_risk=1.75,
    signature_mmd_weight=0.5,
)

expected_returns = sde_estimator.estimate(market_data)
cov_surface = sde_estimator.estimate_covariance(market_data, refit=False)
scenarios_3d = sde_estimator.estimate_scenarios(market_data, refit=False)

docs.title: Time-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Networks (ApolloPFN) & Bayesian Ensemble
docs.text: ApolloPFN (Potapczynski et al., TMLR 2026 / arXiv:2603.15802v2) is a time-series-aware Prior-Data Fitted Network (PFN) that performs zero-shot amortized Bayesian inference in a single forward pass, conditioning jointly on historical target returns, past-only covariates (MarketData.features), and known-future covariates (MarketData.future_features).

docs.title: Strongly-Typed Exogenous Covariates (CovariateKey & CovariateMode)
docs.text:
To prevent macro indicators, COT crowding metrics, and scheduled calendar events from getting lost in magic strings, pyalloq provides CovariateKey and CovariateMode in pyalloq_core.enums. All three foundation families (ApolloPFN, TimesFM-3, and Timestral) call data.extract_covariates() and share 100% interchangeable constructor signatures:

from pyalloq import CovariateKey, CovariateMode, MarketData
from pyalloq.dl import (
    ApolloPFNReturnEstimator,
    ApolloPFNViewGenerator,
    EnsembleReturnEstimator,
    EnsembleViewGenerator,
    TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator,
    TimestralMultivariateReturnEstimator,
)

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,
    features={
        CovariateKey.COT_CROWDING: cot_df,
        CovariateKey.INTEREST_RATES: rates_df,
    },
    future_features={
        CovariateKey.CALENDAR_EVENTS: fomc_cpi_calendar_df,
    },
)

# Interchangeable kwargs across ApolloPFN, TimesFM-3, and Timestral
shared_kwargs = {
    "horizon": 21,
    "annualize": True,
    "covariate_mode": CovariateMode.AUTO,
    "covariate_keys": [
        CovariateKey.COT_CROWDING,
        CovariateKey.INTEREST_RATES,
        CovariateKey.CALENDAR_EVENTS,
    ],
}

apfn_est = ApolloPFNReturnEstimator(model=None, **shared_kwargs)
tfm_est  = TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator(model=tfm_model, **shared_kwargs)
tms_est  = TimestralMultivariateReturnEstimator(model=tms_model, **shared_kwargs)

# Precision-weighted / sCRPS-adaptive / CVaR-adaptive Bayesian Model Averaging
ensemble = EnsembleReturnEstimator(
    estimators=[apfn_est, tfm_est, tms_est],
    weighting_mode="scrps_adaptive",  # or "cvar_adaptive", "inverse_uncertainty"
    copula_type="student_t",
    model_names=["ApolloPFN", "TimesFM-3", "Timestral"],
)
mu_ensemble = ensemble.estimate(data)
print(apfn_est.last_covariate_importance_)  # Zero-shot AttnFeat covariate attribution
print(ensemble.last_posterior_cvar_)        # Exact Riemann Bar Expected Shortfall (CVaR_95%)
print(ensemble.last_posterior_skewness_)    # Non-parametric Bowley decile skewness

# Synthesize Copula-Coupled Riemann Bar 3D Scenarios (BaseScenarioEstimator)
scenarios_3d = ensemble.estimate_scenarios(data, n_paths=100, horizon=21)

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Return Estimator
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.interfaces import BaseReturnEstimator
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyReturnEstimator(BaseReturnEstimator):
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.Series:
        # Annualized mean of log returns
        log_returns = data.prices.apply(lambda col: col.pct_change().add(1).apply(lambda x: x if x > 0 else 1e-6))
        return log_returns.mean() * 252

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=MyReturnEstimator(),
)

docs.title: Strategy Pipeline
docs.text: StrategyPipeline is the orchestrator that connects your return estimator, covariance estimator, and allocator into a single callable unit. It is the primary object consumed by WalkForwardEngine.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

With defaults, StrategyPipeline uses:

  • Return estimator: EWMAReturnEstimator (60-day span)
  • Covariance estimator: EmpiricalCovariance

docs.title: Full Configuration
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.markowitz import MarkowitzAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq_core.enums import ObjectiveFunction

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(
        tickers=data.assets,
        objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE,
    ),
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
    allocator_kwargs={},  # optional extra kwargs forwarded to allocator.allocate()
)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When generate_weights(data) is called — either directly or by the backtest engine — it runs the following sequence:

def generate_weights(self, data: MarketData) -> pd.Series:
    expected_returns = self.returns_estimator.estimate(data)  # → pd.Series (N,)
    cov_matrix       = self.cov_estimator.estimate(data)      # → pd.DataFrame (N×N)

    result = self.allocator.allocate(
        data,
        cov_matrix=cov_matrix,
        expected_returns=expected_returns,
        **self.allocator_kwargs,
    )

    return result.weights  # → pd.Series (N,)

This means the pipeline is fully self-contained: given a MarketData slice, it produces portfolio weights.

docs.title: Using with WalkForwardEngine
docs.text:
The pipeline is the only thing WalkForwardEngine needs to know about your strategy:

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(pipeline=pipeline, rebalance_freq="ME")
results = engine.run(data)

The engine handles windowing, lookahead prevention, and cost accounting. The pipeline handles estimation and optimization.

docs.title: Calling Directly (Without Backtest)
docs.text:
You can also call the pipeline directly to get weights for a given data window, useful for live portfolio construction:

# Use the last 252 days
window_data = data.slice_time(end_date=data.prices.index[-1], lookback=252)
weights = pipeline.generate_weights(window_data)
print(weights)

docs.title: Visualization & Tear Sheets (pyalloq-viz)
docs.text: pyalloq-viz provides an institutional visualization suite for pyalloq. It turns your optimization results, walk-forward backtests, Monte Carlo scenarios, and macroeconomic views into interactive Plotly figures and standalone HTML tear sheet dashboards.

docs.text:
flowchart LR

docs.title: Two Ways to Visualize
docs.text:
1. Granular Plot Functions (plot_*): Every visualization is exposed as a standalone function returning a styled plotly.graph_objects.Figure.
  2. Composite Tear Sheet Classes (*TearSheet): Specialized tear sheet classes group related charts and compute summary KPIs:
  3. SimulationTearSheet: Synthetic path cones, terminal wealth & ruin, CVaR tail shading, and drawdown cones.
  4. RobustnessTearSheet: Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) and Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV) timeline scrambling.
  5. MacroRegimeTearSheet: Meucci Entropy Pooling prior-vs-posterior shifts and GMM Markov regime transition overlays.
  6. AllocationTearSheet: Multi-universe efficient frontier, weight drift & turnover, hierarchical treemaps, component risk contributions, and correlation/monthly return heatmaps.
  7. ComparisonTearSheet: Multi-strategy equity & drawdown overlays, multi-allocator probabilistic cones & terminal wealth KDEs, intra-rebalance sawtooth weight drift & turnover bars, and Brinson-Fachler / Factor / Frictional Drag waterfalls with Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) KPIs.

docs.title: 1. The Multiverse & Simulation Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Evaluates synthetic futures (ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult), supporting both uniform scenario weights and view-adjusted posterior probabilities (EntropyResult).

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_fan_chart Median & expected equity trajectories enveloped by probability-weighted percentile bands (5–95, 10–90, 25–75) + spaghetti paths ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult, optional EntropyResult, optional benchmark plot_terminal_wealth_ruin Terminal wealth density & histogram with shaded left-tail ruin region below 1 + ruin_threshold ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult, ruin_threshold (e.g. -0.20) plot_cvar_tail_risk Return distribution with vertical markers at \(\text{VaR}_\alpha\) and \(\text{CVaR}_\alpha\) (Expected Shortfall) and shaded tail shortfall mass ScenarioMarketData, MonteCarloResult, or BacktestResult, alpha=0.05 plot_drawdown_fan_chart Underwater drawdown probability bands across all \(M\) synthetic trajectories ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult, optional EntropyResult SimulationTearSheet Combines all 4 charts into a 2×2 figure or HTML dashboard with 7 summary KPIs All of the above TearSheet DashboardIndividual Plot Functions 
from pyalloq_simulation import GMMRegimeGenerator, ViewBuilder, AbsoluteView, EntropyPooler
from pyalloq_viz import SimulationTearSheet

# 1. Generate 500 synthetic paths over 63 trading days
gen = GMMRegimeGenerator(n_regimes=2, random_state=42)
gen.fit(market_data)
scenarios = gen.generate(n_paths=500, horizon=63)

# 2. Optional: Apply Entropy Pooling views
builder = ViewBuilder(scenarios)
A, b, C, d = builder.build([AbsoluteView(asset="AAPL", operator=">=", target=0.02)])
entropy_res = EntropyPooler(n_scenarios=scenarios.n_paths).fit(A_ineq=A, b_ineq=b, C_eq=C, d_eq=d)

# 3. Build & export the Simulation Tear Sheet
sim_ts = SimulationTearSheet(
    scenarios,
    asset_weights=backtest_result.weights.iloc[-1],
    entropy_result=entropy_res,
    ruin_threshold=-0.15,
    cvar_alpha=0.05,
    benchmark=backtest_result,
)

sim_ts.show()                              # Render 2x2 Plotly figure
sim_ts.to_html("simulation_report.html")   # Save standalone HTML dashboard

from pyalloq_viz import (
    plot_fan_chart,
    plot_terminal_wealth_ruin,
    plot_cvar_tail_risk,
    plot_drawdown_fan_chart,
)

fig_fan  = plot_fan_chart(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res, benchmark=backtest_result)
fig_ruin = plot_terminal_wealth_ruin(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res, ruin_threshold=-0.15)
fig_cvar = plot_cvar_tail_risk(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res, alpha=0.05)
fig_dd   = plot_drawdown_fan_chart(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res)

docs.title: 2. Robustness & Overfitting Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Proves whether a strategy's historical performance is genuinely robust or an artifact of backtest overfitting and chronological luck, powered by PBOEvaluator and CPCVSplitter in pyalloq_backtest.

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_pbo_distribution CSCV Mode: Rank logit (\(\lambda_c\)) KDE with shaded overfitting mass (\(\lambda_c \le 0\)) + In-Sample vs. Out-of-Sample Sharpe degradation regression.Benchmark Mode: Simulated/CPCV Sharpe distribution vs. historical backtest Sharpe + survival ECDF. PBOResult, (T, M) trial matrix, or BacktestResult + CPCVResult/MonteCarloResult plot_cpcv_paths Recombined combinatorial timelines scrambling the chronological order of market regimes + path-level Sharpe vs. Max Drawdown scatter CPCVResult or BacktestResult RobustnessTearSheet Unified 2×2 overfitting & regime-scrambling dashboard with PBO, OOS loss probability, and CPCV survival KPIs BacktestResult, PBOResult, or (T, M) trial matrix Single-Strategy CPCV & Benchmark ModeMulti-Strategy CSCV Matrix Mode 
from pyalloq_backtest import CPCVSplitter
from pyalloq_viz import RobustnessTearSheet, plot_cpcv_paths, plot_pbo_distribution

# Scramble historical strategy returns across 6 chronological regime blocks
splitter = CPCVSplitter(n_groups=6, k_test_groups=2, max_paths=100)
cpcv_result = splitter.scramble_timelines(backtest_result)

# Individual plots:
fig_cpcv = plot_cpcv_paths(cpcv_result)
fig_pbo  = plot_pbo_distribution(backtest_result, synthetic_comparison=cpcv_result)

# Full Tear Sheet:
rob_ts = RobustnessTearSheet(backtest_result, cpcv_or_synthetic=cpcv_result)
rob_ts.to_html("robustness_report.html")

from pyalloq_backtest import PBOEvaluator
from pyalloq_viz import RobustnessTearSheet, plot_pbo_distribution

# Evaluate M candidate strategy configurations across S=8 combinatorial partitions
# strategy_trials_df has shape (T_days, M_trials)
pbo_eval = PBOEvaluator(n_partitions=8)
pbo_result = pbo_eval.evaluate_cscv(strategy_trials_df)

print(f"Probability of Backtest Overfitting: {pbo_result.pbo:.1%}")
fig = plot_pbo_distribution(pbo_result)

# Or generate the complete Tear Sheet directly from the (T, M) DataFrame:
RobustnessTearSheet(strategy_trials_df, n_partitions=8).to_html("cscv_pbo_report.html")

docs.title: 3. Macro Regime & Entropy Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Visualizes how subjective macroeconomic views warp the probability distribution of synthetic scenarios (EntropyPooler) and how portfolios behave across latent Gaussian Mixture Markov regimes (GMMRegimeGenerator).

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_entropy_pooling Left Panel: Uniform prior \(p_m = 1/M\) vs. sorted posterior \(x^*_m\) with KL Divergence and Effective Number of Scenarios (\(\text{ENS}\)).Right Panel: Prior vs. view-shifted posterior return density. EntropyResult, optional ScenarioMarketData plot_regime_transitions Historical Mode: Equity curve with dominant regime background shading + real-time posterior regime probabilities \(p_k(t)\).Synthetic Mode: Simulated equity cone + cross-sectional proportion of paths in each Markov state. BacktestResult or ScenarioMarketData, GMMRegimeGenerator MacroRegimeTearSheet Combines Entropy Pooling diagnostics and GMM regime transition overlays into a single report EntropyResult, BacktestResult or ScenarioMarketData, GMMRegimeGenerator TearSheet DashboardIndividual Plot Functions 
from pyalloq_viz import MacroRegimeTearSheet

macro_ts = MacroRegimeTearSheet(
    entropy_result=entropy_res,
    equity_or_scenarios=backtest_result,
    gmm_or_probs=gen,
    scenario_data=scenarios,
    market_data=market_data,
)
macro_ts.to_html("macro_regime_report.html")

from pyalloq_viz import plot_entropy_pooling, plot_regime_transitions

# 1. Entropy Pooling Prior vs. Posterior
fig_ep = plot_entropy_pooling(entropy_res, scenario_data=scenarios)

# 2. Historical Equity Curve with Decoded GMM Regime Shading
fig_hist_reg = plot_regime_transitions(
    backtest_result,
    gmm_or_probs=gen,
    market_data=market_data,
)

# 3. Synthetic Multiverse Markov State Proportions
fig_sim_reg = plot_regime_transitions(scenarios, gmm_or_probs=gen)

docs.title: 4. Allocation Mechanics & Risk Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Provides deep visibility into optimizer geometry, intra-rebalance weight drift, hierarchical clustering structure, risk parity budgets, and seasonal return patterns.

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_multi_universe_frontier Parametric Markowitz frontier + random Dirichlet portfolio cloud + optimal allocations solved across synthetic scenarios expected_returns, cov_matrix, optional scenario_data & allocator_or_pipeline plot_weight_drift_turnover Reconstructs daily intra-rebalance drifted weights (sawtooth drift + rebalance snap-backs) and two-way rebalance turnover bars BacktestResult, MarketData plot_hierarchical_composition Multi-level Treemap (Portfolio -> Sector/Cluster -> Asset) + Current vs. Target/Benchmark horizontal bar chart OptimizationResult or pd.Series, optional target_or_benchmark_weights, MarketData plot_risk_contributions Capital weights (\(w_i\)) vs. Percentage Component Risk Contributions (\(\text{PCRC}_i\)) vs. Target Risk Budgets (\(b_i\)) OptimizationResult or pd.Series, cov_matrix plot_correlation_and_periodic_returns Quasi-diagonalized asset correlation heatmap + Year × Month (Jan–Dec) periodic return heatmap with annual totals MarketData or cov_matrix, BacktestResult AllocationTearSheet Combines allocation, risk parity, drift, and correlation diagnostics into a unified report All of the above TearSheet DashboardIndividual Plot Functions 
from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.hrp import HRPAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_budgeting import RiskBudgetingAllocator
from pyalloq_viz import AllocationTearSheet

cov = market_data.get_returns().cov() * 252.0
mu  = market_data.get_returns().mean() * 252.0

hrp = HRPAllocator(tickers=market_data.assets)
hrp_res = hrp.allocate(market_data, cov_matrix=cov)
rb_res  = RiskBudgetingAllocator(tickers=market_data.assets).allocate(market_data, cov_matrix=cov)

alloc_ts = AllocationTearSheet(
    optimization_result=hrp_res,
    backtest_result=backtest_result,
    market_data=market_data,
    cov_matrix=cov,
    expected_returns=mu,
    scenario_data=scenarios,
    allocator_or_pipeline=hrp,
    target_weights=rb_res,
)
alloc_ts.to_html("allocation_report.html")

from pyalloq_viz import (
    plot_multi_universe_frontier,
    plot_weight_drift_turnover,
    plot_hierarchical_composition,
    plot_risk_contributions,
    plot_correlation_and_periodic_returns,
)

fig_ef   = plot_multi_universe_frontier(mu, cov, scenario_data=scenarios, allocator_or_pipeline=hrp, optimal_portfolios=[hrp_res, rb_res])
fig_wd   = plot_weight_drift_turnover(backtest_result, market_data=market_data)
fig_tree = plot_hierarchical_composition(hrp_res, target_or_benchmark_weights=rb_res, market_data=market_data)
fig_rc   = plot_risk_contributions(rb_res, cov_matrix=cov)
fig_corr = plot_correlation_and_periodic_returns(market_data, portfolio_returns=backtest_result)

docs.title: 5. Multi-Strategy Comparison & Attribution Tear Sheet (ComparisonTearSheet)
docs.text:
Visualizes how multiple allocators (BenchmarkSuite / MultiStrategyComparator) navigate identical market regimes and synthetic realities while decomposing active return and execution frictions.

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_equity_drawdown_overlay Cumulative net-of-cost equity curves overlaid with underwater drawdown charts and systemic regime stress highlights ComparisonResult or Mapping[str, BacktestResult], optional benchmark plot_multi_strategy_fan_chart Multi-strategy median equity curves enveloped by 10th–90th and 25th–75th percentile confidence cones + terminal wealth KDEs ComparisonResult or Mapping[str, MonteCarloResult | BacktestResult], optional scenario_data plot_multi_turnover_drift Daily intra-rebalance sawtooth weight drift ((\sum_i w_{i,t}^- - w_{i,\text{target}} plot_attribution_waterfall Left Panel: Brinson-Fachler (Allocation, Selection, Interaction) & Factor Alpha.Right Panel: Gross-to-Net Frictional Drag Waterfall (Paper -> Drift/Decay -> Spread -> Market Impact -> Net). ComparisonResult, AttributionResult, or Mapping[str, AttributionResult] ComparisonTearSheet Unified 2×2 dashboard and HTML report with Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR), Trial Count (\(N\)), Top Factor Alpha, and Drawdown KPIs ComparisonResult or Mapping[str, BacktestResult] TearSheet DashboardIndividual Plot Functions 
from pyalloq_backtest import BenchmarkSuite
from pyalloq_viz import ComparisonTearSheet

comp_result = BenchmarkSuite(pipelines=pipelines, benchmark="EqualWeight").run(
    market_data, scenario_data=scenarios
)

comp_ts = ComparisonTearSheet(
    comp_result,
    market_data=market_data,
    scenario_data=scenarios,
    benchmark=comp_result.results["EqualWeight"],
)
comp_ts.show()
comp_ts.to_html("multi_strategy_comparison_report.html")

from pyalloq_viz import (
    plot_equity_drawdown_overlay,
    plot_multi_strategy_fan_chart,
    plot_multi_turnover_drift,
    plot_attribution_waterfall,
)

fig_eq   = plot_equity_drawdown_overlay(comp_result, benchmark=comp_result.results["EqualWeight"])
fig_cone = plot_multi_strategy_fan_chart(comp_result, scenario_data=scenarios)
fig_to   = plot_multi_turnover_drift(comp_result, market_data=market_data)
fig_attr = plot_attribution_waterfall(comp_result, market_data=market_data)

docs.title: 6. Spectral Contagion Network & Hawkes Fragility Regime Portraits
docs.text:
Visualizes the market Graph Laplacian topology (\(\mathcal{L}_t = I - D_t^{-1/2}W_t D_t^{-1/2}\)), Fiedler vector (\(v_2\)) spectral bisection partitions, Wiener-Hopf Hawkes branching out-degrees, and rolling structural fragility diagnostics (\(\lambda_2(t)\), \(\rho(G_t)\), and effective Hurst \(H_{\text{eff}}(t)\)):

import pandas as pd
from pyalloq import ReactionDiffusionCovarianceEstimator
from pyalloq_viz import (
    plot_fragility_hawkes_regime_portrait,
    plot_spectral_contagion_network,
)

rd_est = ReactionDiffusionCovarianceEstimator(slow_window=60)
cov_df = rd_est.estimate(market_data)

adj_df = pd.DataFrame(
    rd_est.last_adjacency_,
    index=market_data.assets,
    columns=market_data.assets,
)
fig_net = plot_spectral_contagion_network(
    adjacency=adj_df,
    branching_matrix=rd_est.hawkes_branching_matrix_,
)
fig_net.show()

docs.title: 7. Set Transformer Inducing Factor, Spectral Conditioning & Cardinality Diagnostics
docs.text:
plot_set_transformer_diagnostics renders a 3-panel interactive Plotly figure inspecting SetTransformerCovarianceNet and SetTransformerPolicyNet:

  1. Panel 1 (ISAB Inducing Factor Loadings \(B_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times m}\)): Heatmap of learned dynamic latent risk factor exposures across assets.
  2. Panel 2 (Eigenvalue Spectrum & Conditioning \(\kappa\)): Log-scale eigenvalue spectrum comparing lower-triangular Cholesky vs. ISABFactorDiagonalHead and RIESpectralHead cleaning.
  3. Panel 3 (Cardinality-Shift Concentration Stability): Top position weight (\(\max_i w_i\)) across universe sizes \(N \in [10, 1000]\) comparing Standard Softmax dilution against Scalable-Softmax (SSMax) and CappedSimplexProjection.
from pyalloq.dl import DeepCovarianceEstimator, SetTransformerCovarianceNet
from pyalloq_viz import plot_set_transformer_diagnostics

set_cov = SetTransformerCovarianceNet(n_features=1, hidden_dim=32, num_inds=4)
est = DeepCovarianceEstimator(model=set_cov, lookback_window=20, allow_ragged=True)
factor_loadings_df, _, _ = est.estimate_factors(market_data)

fig_set = plot_set_transformer_diagnostics(
    factor_loadings=factor_loadings_df,
    eigenvalue_spectra={"ISAB_Factor_Diag": [2.4, 1.1, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3]},
)
fig_set.show()

docs.title: Themes & Static Exports
docs.text:
Every plot function and tear sheet supports two built-in institutional themes:

  • "alloq_dark" (default): Slate/obsidian background (#0B0F19) with high-contrast emerald, cyan, amber, coral, crimson, and violet semantic accents.
  • "alloq_light": Clean publication white/slate background (#FFFFFF) tailored for PDFs and print reports.
from pyalloq_viz import plot_fan_chart, apply_plotly_theme

# Pass theme directly to any plot function or TearSheet method
fig = plot_fan_chart(scenarios, theme="alloq_light")

# Or re-style an existing Plotly or Matplotlib figure
apply_plotly_theme(fig, theme="alloq_dark", title="Custom Title", subtitle="Custom Subtitle")
